en: The Svayambhūpurāṇa, Chapter One:
The Narrative of the Origin of the Self-Existent Dharmadhātu.

Oṃ, homage to the glorious Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara and to all the Buddhas, Dharmas, and Bodhisattvas! I, taking refuge, pay homage to that glorious Great Buddha, the mass of splendor, by whom the True Dharma was fully revealed throughout the three worlds. Svayambhū Purāṇa 1.1.
Having bowed to the Lord of the three worlds, the abode of the Victors of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), I shall speak this summary of the Self-Arisen One; listen with reverence.
That bodhisattva who listens with faith to this sublime narrative of the self-arisen one’s birth will certainly become one whose three bodies are completely purified.
Thus, in former times, the son of the Sugata named Jayaśrī, who was a master of the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*),
dwelt at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) together with his community of monks.
There, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati named Jineśvara,
having gone for refuge with faith, should take recourse in Jayaśrī.
Then that wise Jayaśrī, who knows how to act for the benefit of all sentient beings,
took his place upon the throne in the assembly hall in order to teach the true Dharma.
Therein were all the great beings, the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Conquerors,
as well as Arhats, monks, and celibate disciples.
Nun priestesses who observe the holy life, laymen who keep their vows, as well as laywomen and other great crowds of householders; Svayambhūpurāṇa 1.8.
Brahmins, those devoted to sacred fords, ascetics, and practitioners of austerity;
kings, ministers, counselors, commanders of the army, and the citizens.
Villagers, country folk, and likewise people dwelling elsewhere,
arrived with faith to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
There, having respectfully honored and bowed to that Arhat Jayaśrī as he sat in the assembly, [the king] proceeded in due order within that gathering.
With palms joined in reverence, they all surrounded him on every side;
placing him at their head and gazing up at him, they took refuge in him with concentrated minds.
Seeing them all seated together, eager to hear the true Dharma,
the Bodhisattva Jinaśrī rose up.
Wearing his upper garment and resting with palms joined in reverence, he knelt upon the ground with both knees and, gazing [at him], spoke thus: Svayambhū Purāṇa 1.14.
"Venerable sir, I desire to practice the vow of awakening;
therefore, having first undertaken what vow should I proceed with a concentrated mind? (SvayambhuP 1.15)
Therefore, may you, having instructed us all and awakening us,
be worthy of leading us by uniting us with the path to enlightenment through auspicious deeds.
Having heard what was thus requested by him, Jayaśrī, the son of the Sugata, addressed that Mahāsattva with these words in the assembly: Svayambhūpurāṇa 1.17.
Listen, child; if you have a desire for the vow of perfect awakening, I shall explain to you, in due order, the means of accomplishing the vow of perfect awakening.
Whoever desires to practice the vow of awakening within that cycle of existence should first go for refuge and rely upon a true spiritual teacher.
Having received that instruction, being composed and according to his knowledge, he practiced.
Having bathed at the sacred ford, with a purified soul and having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
he worshipped according to the ritual rules, his intention fixed upon perfect enlightenment.
Having undertaken the vow of the Upoṣadha, one should practice it for the welfare of the world;
thus, the wise person whose mind is set on perfect enlightenment should always conduct themselves.
That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who bears the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, shall possess the three perfectly pure bodies.
Being composed in meditative absorption, he should gradually fulfill the equipment for perfect enlightenment;
his self being devoted to this merit, he maintains the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras).
Free from afflictions and having conquered Māra, he shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Thus, manifesting the true Dharma throughout all worlds,
and having completed the work of the Sugata, he shall attain perfect nirvāṇa.
Then, having become an Arhat and a Sugata, awakening all sentient beings and establishing them on the path to enlightenment, he should cause them to practice within the conventional realm.
In this way, all the perfectly awakened ones— those who have passed away, those yet to come,
and those existing in the present— arise from the ripening of the merit of this vow.
The Victors have attained awakening, they will attain it, and they are attaining it;
so too are all the Mahāsattvas, the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Victors.
Likewise, all Arhats, having purified the three spheres, have attained awakening and entered perfect nirvāṇa; they will enter it, and they are entering it now.
Having understood this, whenever you desire perfect peace,
go for refuge to the Three Jewels and practice this vow.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, that son of the Sugata, looking intently at the Arhat Jineśvara, spoke as follows: Svayambhūpurāṇa 1.32.
"Venerable Sir, I wish to hear about that supreme place for observing vows; please instruct me on that region where one should practice this vow."
When he had thus prayed, Jayaśrī, that great-minded one, beholding the Victorious Lord, the Great Being, gave this instruction: Svayambhūpurāṇa 1.34.
Listen attentively, my child, to this most excellent place of observance;
I shall now describe it to you exactly as it was proclaimed by the lords of sages.
In fields of merit, at sacred fords, in monasteries, and in the hermitages of the Sugatas.
And [one should offer] at the shrines (caityas) and images of the Buddhas and those who have attained cessation (nivṛta).
In all Buddha-fields, the place of abiding in the vow is most excellent;
among these, the self-arisen caitya is proclaimed to be supreme.
Having understood this, the wise person who desires to practice the vow should rely upon the field of the Self-Existent Victor and practice that vow. (SvayambhuP 1.38)
He who joyfully undertakes and practices a vow while residing in the field of Svayambhū shall obtain that great,
inexhaustible merit which is the means for achieving enlightenment.
This merit, O Bhadraśrī, belongs to one who is pure in soul and a refuge for excellent virtues;
he is certainly a Bodhisattva of great supernormal powers, a son of the Victors, and eternal.
He shall never at any time go to an evil rebirth anywhere within cyclic existence;
always born into a happy state, he shall practice the vow of the conduct of awakening.
Thus wandering through the world, having practiced benevolence everywhere and maintained the vow for perfect awakening, he moved about for the welfare of that world.
And thus, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
and having attained the threefold enlightenment, one shall reach the state of final liberation.
Having thus understood this,
take refuge in the Three Jewels and, relying upon the state of the Self-Existent One, practice the supreme vow.
Having heard this which was taught by the Arhat, that son of the Sugata, looking intently at the Arhat Jayaśrī, spoke as follows: Svayambhūpurāṇa 1.45.
"Venerable sir, having heard what you have taught, it pleases my mind;
I wish to observe the vow after having worshipped the self-arisen caitya."
Where in this world of earth is the self-arisen king of caityas, the glorious Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Jinas? It behoves you to point that out.
Having heard this request made by him, that wise Arhat ascetic, Jayaśrī, looked upon the Great Being and instructed him as follows: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 1.48.
In this world of men, on the Himalayas in the north,
there exists in the renowned land of Nepal a supreme mountain named Gopuccha.
The name of that mountain changes fourfold throughout the four yugas;
for instance, in the Kṛta-yuga, it was known as Padmagiri.
In the Tretā age he was known as Vajrakūṭa, and in the Dvāpara age he is remembered as Gośṛṅga;
but now, in the Kali age, he is renowned as Gopuccha.
That very Śaila is now renowned among the people of the land of Nepal as Sāṃheguri; thus he has established himself upon the earth.
That [place] consists of all elements beginning with earth, is said to be composed of all substances,
and is beautifully adorned with all kinds of trees, foremost among which is the Aśvattha.
Everywhere it was lovely with flowers, with trees bearing all kinds of medicinal herbs and fruits,
with the warbling of all manner of birds, and with the humming of wandering bees.
It was inhabited by all creatures whose minds were bound by affection and friendship,
who lived like ascetics, and who moved about with auspicious conduct.
It was adorned with cascades of pure nectar endowed with the eight qualities,
and with breezes perfumed by the excellence of flowers and fragrances.
He is always attended by those of divine and great energy,
and is constantly served with reverence by the lords of all the worlds.
There, a lotus made of jewels rests upon the pericarp;
it is stainless, possessing the nature of light with the luster of divine crystal-jewels.
One cubit in height and in the form of a caitya,
this self-arisen shrine of the Jina stands for the welfare of all worlds.
[He is] by Brahmā, Śakra, and all the other gods, by all the lords of the worlds,
by all the lords of the Daityas, and also by the lords of the Nāgas and the Garuḍas.
By the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Sādhyas, Uragas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
by the lords of the Rākṣasas, the Rudras, the Grahas, and even the hosts of stars.
By the Vasus and the Apsarases, by all the lords of the thirty-three gods,
by all the ṛṣis, the ascetics, the yogins, and the celibate students.
He was seen, remembered, and honored day and night, at the four junctions of the day, by all the learned heterodox teachers, ascetics, and virtuous people.
Whenever he arrived, [the king] would always worship him with great respect,
honoring and saluting him with hymns of praise and great enthusiasm.
Thus that Lord of the Three Worlds, the Self-Existent One who is the Dharmadhātu,
remained engaged in conversation for the sake of the welfare of all the world.
But now, in the Kali age, people will be wicked, cruel-minded, and deceitful;
having seen this Dharma-realm of the Self-Existent One, they will surely seize it—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, having covered it with stone and made it secure, he revealed it;
and having constructed a supreme *caitya* over it with bricks, he established it.
Having adorned it with umbrellas, banners, and flags, they both took their seats there,
as did all the people and all the lords of the world.
Having approached, propitiated, and honored him,
he was saluted with great enthusiasm through offerings, hymns of praise, circumambulations, and other such ceremonies.
Thus, having propitiated him with prostrations, that Lord of the Three Worlds— the Dharmadhātu and abode of the Victors— was served, honored, and worshipped.
It stands there, beautifully adorned for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings;
those who go to it for refuge proceed with pure joy.
They never go to an evil rebirth here in this saṃsāra;
they are born only in happy states, adorned by the Dharma and graced by the Saṅgha.
The Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, whose three spheres are completely purified,
are auspicious, glorious, possessors of excellent qualities, and benefactors of all sentient beings.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, he moved about for the welfare of the world;
in this same way, you too, having understood this, have gone for refuge with faith.
Having propitiated the Svayambhū-caitya, always observe the vow;
by doing so, you shall attain auspicious glory in this saṃsāra as a refuge for virtuous qualities.
You shall become Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, and sons of the Victors;
thereafter, having fulfilled the equipment for perfect enlightenment in due order.
"Having attained the threefold enlightenment, you two shall reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction from him, that Mahāmati—
Beholding that Teacher, he spoke again in this way:
"Venerable One, I wish to hear what the Self-Existent One, the Abode of the Victors, has said."
"When did you yourself arise, and how did you teach that?
Having heard this request from him, that wise Arhat ascetic [replied].
Beholding that Great Being, Jayaśrī instructed him as follows:
"Excellent! Listen, O illustrious one, to how I have heard it from my teacher."
Thus I shall relate to you the excellent narrative of the self-arisen one's birth:
namely, how in the city of Pāṭaliputra there was a king named Aśoka.
He became one who was zealous in accomplishing the true Dharma and a devotee of the Three Jewels;
he resided there in that monastery of the Kukkuṭārāma, the hermitage of the Sugata.
He proceeded to pay homage to Upagupta, who possessed great supernormal powers;
at that time, that Arhat of great supernormal powers was preceded by the entire Saṅgha.
Seated in the midst of the assembly, he remained there composed in meditation;
and all the community, placing him at their head, attended upon that Arhat seated in the hall.
Seeing them, that lord of the earth, Aśoka, was delighted and approached;
having gone there suddenly with palms joined in reverence, he attended upon the Arhats, the ascetics.
Having bowed to Upagupta with his entire body, he joyfully prostrated before that venerable Arhat with the eight limbs of reverence,
according to the prescribed rite and with great enthusiasm.
Having worshipped and prostrated, he sat down to listen to the Dharma;
likewise did all his ministers, along with the counselors and officials.
Having bowed to that Arhat ascetic, he took refuge in a secluded spot there;
then that Arhat, possessed of great supernormal knowledge, saw all those who had gathered around him.
He taught the true Dharma, auspicious in its beginning, middle, and end;
having drunk that nectar of the true Dharma, all the worlds were awakened.
Having understood the distinction of the Dharma, they desired the vow of perfect enlightenment;
then that great king also, having heard that supreme Dharma, [did the same].
He desired to practice the conduct that accomplishes perfect enlightenment;
then that king, the ruler of men, approached him with palms joined in reverence.
Having bowed to that Arhat Mahāsattva and gazing upon him with joy, he said:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear the vow that accomplishes perfect enlightenment."
Where is the most meritorious field where a vow is swiftly fulfilled?
May you instruct us on that, awakening all the worlds.
Having yoked himself to the path to enlightenment, he ought to proceed along it.
When the king had thus made his request, that Arhat Mahāmati, having heard it...
Beholding King Aśoka, he spoke thus:
"Excellent! Listen, O Great King, to how it was declared by my preceptor."
Thus I shall declare to you the vow of awakening, O King, best of all kṣatriyas, if you so desire; it is located in the north, in the Himalayas.
In that place known as Nepal, where a vow is swiftly accomplished,
there too is a most great field of merit praised by the Buddhas.
In that place, which is the support of the Dharmadhātu, the sovereign caitya of the Self-Existent One,
whatever action is performed is swiftly brought to fulfillment.
Thus it has been cultivated by all the Great Beings and even by the Victors;
having understood this, O Lord of Kings, if you desire perfect enlightenment— ||| Svayambhūpurāṇa 1.99 |||
Having gone for refuge to that caitya, practice the excellent restraint;
thus, with a self purified by this merit, O Bhadraśrī, you shall possess the supernatural power of noble qualities.
May you become a Bodhisattva of great supernormal knowledge, bearing the welfare and benefit of all;
then, gradually fulfilling the accumulations for perfect enlightenment.
"Free from afflictions, O Arhat, Lord of the World, you shall attain the state of a Perfectly Awakened One.
Having heard this prediction from that Arhat, the king was filled with joy.
Having bowed to his teacher Upagupta, he asked with great reverence:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear the excellent narrative concerning the origin of the Self-Existent One."
Having heard the king’s request, "When will he himself arise so that he may instruct us? that arhat ascetic of noble intelligence replied:
Beholding King Aśoka, he spoke thus:
"Excellent, O King! I have heard exactly what was instructed by my preceptor."
Thus I shall fully proclaim; listen to that with a concentrated mind.
At that time, he was the Teacher of the World, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
The omniscient King of Dharma, the Arhat, Lord of Sages, and Guide— he,
together with his monastic community, was wandering through the inhabited lands.
At one time, he arrived there in Nepal,
on the western side of Mount Gopuccha, near Śrī Svayambhū.
In the vicinity of the Abhidha-caitya at the Sugata’s hermitage,
he shone like the full moon for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
When that Blessed One, the Teacher, dwelt together with his assembly in order to fully teach the True Dharma for the increase of the Dharma among sentient beings, [he remained there].
He took his seat upon the assembly throne to fully teach the True Dharma; seeing him there at that time in my hermitage, Mañjuśrī—*Svayambhū Purāṇa* 1.111.
Residing in a monastery, named Cūḍā, she was a celibate practitioner;
an Arhatī, a Bhikṣuṇī, auspicious, and desirous of the qualities of the True Dharma.
With a perfectly serene basis, pure and clad in saffron robes,
she was filled with joy as she took up the divine offerings and services.
Then, those great beings, the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Victors, quickly approached that place in order to drink the nectar of his true Dharma.
All those headed by Maitreya have come to hear that Dharma—
the Arhats, the monks, the disciples, and those who lead the holy life.
There were bhikṣuṇīs practicing celibacy, as well as cailakas and those observing vows;
there were laymen and laywomen who took refuge in the Three Jewels.
All those devoted to the worship of the Buddha, having come to hear his Dharma,
all assembled there and took their seats in the assembly hall.
Beholding that Perfectly Awakened One, they approached him with joy;
having honored that Protector and bowed with palms joined in delight, they all paid him homage.
To drink that nectar of the True Dharma,
the gods such as Brahmā and Śakra, as well as all the lords of the worlds, took their seats in his assembly.
The planets, the hosts of stars, as well as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas,
Sādhyas, Rudras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Kinnaras.
The lords of the Daityas, the lords of the Rākṣasas, the lords of the Nāgas, and even the Garuḍas—
likewise all other lords of the worlds— arrived there with joy.
Having worshipped and bowed down to that Lord of Sages, they took refuge there;
and Hāritī, the Yakṣiṇī who protects the Bodhisattvas, did so as well.
Having drawn you there, she took refuge in that assembly;
then the Blessed One, the Teacher, saw that everyone had taken their seats.
Having addressed Maitreya and looking intently at him, he commanded as follows:
"O Maitreya, [worship] this Lord of the World, the Self-Existent One, the Abode of the Victors."
Behold with reverence this Dharmadhātu as the Three Jewels;
having gone there, take refuge joyfully and always honor them with faith.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, they move about for the welfare of the world;
those who, with faith, resort to this refuge and take their stand therein.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, they move about for the welfare of the world;
all those have been liberated from evil, their three spheres being completely pure.
May the bodhisattvas possess the great superknowledges and be the locus of excellent qualities;
may they be endowed with auspicious glory and happiness, and abide in the four divine abodes.
Dedicated to the welfare of all sentient beings and practicing the vow of supreme enlightenment,
they never go to an evil rebirth, but always arise in a fortunate state of existence.
Zealous in honoring the Three Jewels and striving to practice the True Dharma,
they then went forth into homelessness and took refuge in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Having undertaken the vow of celibacy, they should move about with concentrated minds;
thereby, their souls become stainless, free from afflictions, and their senses are fully conquered.
Having attained the threefold enlightenment, they shall become fully awakened lotuses;
thus having understood this, those mortals who desire the state of the Sugata [should practice].
"Let them always resort to this very place with faith, taking refuge [in it],"—
having heard these and other words thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, those present in the assembly [acted accordingly].
All the worlds, rejoicing, likewise desired to worship him;
then that wise Bodhisattva Maitreya was indeed filled with joy.
Rising up, he approached the presence of the Lord of Sages;
wearing his upper garment over one shoulder, he bowed down to that Sovereign of Munis.

Joining his knees upon the ground and with palms pressed together, he spoke this to the Blessed One, the Protector, the Omniscient One, the Victor who is the abode of the *dharmadhātu*: (Svayambhūpurāṇa 1.136)
"When will he, having arisen spontaneously,
deign to instruct us?"— thus was it prayed by that great-souled Maitreya.
Beholding the Blessed One, the Greatly Wise, he spoke thus:
"Listen well with a concentrated mind, O Maitreya, self-arisen one."
I shall relate the account of his origin for the awakening of all the world:
in former times, during this Bhadrakalpa, there was an omniscient one named Vipaśyin.
The Teacher of the World, the Lord of Sages, the Arhat, the King of Dharma,
the Tathāgata [appeared] when the maximum lifespan of humans was eighty thousand years.
At that time, it is said, I was a Bodhisattva named Satyadharmākhyā,
when that Blessed One, the Teacher, was in the vicinity of the city of Vandyumatī.
He dwelt in the monastery, teaching the Dharma together with his assembly;
at that time, I attended upon and propitiated that Lord of the World.
Then there arose here a lake seven *kośas* in length and breadth;
having undertaken his instruction, I practiced the vow of awakening (*bodhisamvara*).
Endowed with the eight qualities, it was a reservoir of water surrounded by mountains,
beautified by various fragrant flowers such as lotuses and water-lilies.
It was adorned with flocks of birds headed by swans, cranes, and ducks;
and its banks were lined with trees growing on the slopes that flowered in all seasons.
It was adorned on all sides by trees bearing fruits and medicinal herbs,
and by aquatic creatures such as fish, tortoises, and frogs.
It is an unfathomable abode for living beings and the dwelling place of all the lords of the nāgas;
there resides the great sovereign of all serpent-kings, known by the name Karkkoṭaka.
Thus, at that time, the great sacred ford shone as a refuge for the nectar of merit;
there, the gods were always delighted by the celestial nymphs of the True Dharma.
Having bathed and sported together, they enjoyed sublime happiness and went to heaven;
likewise did all the great sages, beginning with Brahmā, who were rich in asceticism.
Having performed their daily rites such as bathing and the twilight prayers, they always attended [upon him];
likewise, the lords of the world, having bathed here, always remained joyful.
Having honored [the deity] within their respective lineages, they attended upon him with great enthusiasm;
likewise, other people as well, observing vows and living as celibate students, did the same.
Having bathed here and maintained their vows, those with purified souls went to heaven;
likewise, many Bodhisattvas joyfully performed bathing, giving, and observance of vows.
Having established pure conduct here for the welfare of the world,
all the lords of sages likewise [attained] the fruit of the seed of bathing, vows, and other practices.
This most excellent means for accomplishing enlightenment is declared to be of the greatest merit;
having bathed therein, they take refuge in the Three Jewels.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, they acted for the welfare of the world;
those pure-souled ones were swiftly endowed with auspicious glory and excellent qualities.
There were Bodhisattvas, great beings, sons of the Sugatas;
some had purified themselves of afflictions and were free from desire for wandering through existence.
Having approached the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, they became practitioners of celibacy;
some, with stainless souls, turned away from their reliance upon cyclic existence.
Having attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, some reached complete nirvāṇa;
others, longing for the true Dharma, attained the mind set on perfect awakening.
Having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening and practicing for the welfare of the world,
some [beings], having enjoyed all the pleasures of divine sensual desires, [attain liberation].
Devoted to the qualities of the true Dharma, all those rulers of the earth always practiced what was auspicious;
they were all practitioners of righteousness and sound policy.
Having accomplished deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, they finally went to the abode of the Victors;
I too, having bathed there at that time, always practiced the vow.
With his soul purified by this merit, he swiftly attained perfect enlightenment;
and those who drank his water were likewise liberated from their sins.
With pure intentions, these auspicious ones became partakers of enlightenment;
thus was this great sacred site [frequented] by all the lords of sages.
Having been consecrated and praised even today upon the surface of the earth,
the Dharmadhātu himself will certainly arise there hereafter.
Having thus instructed [them], that Lord of Sages further commanded them there in the Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Jinas, which had then arisen.
Free from calamity and filled with auspicious energy, it shall prevail at all times;
and all the worlds, having beheld him, the self-arisen Dharmadhātu, [shall rejoice].
Having gone for refuge with faith, they will always practice [the teachings];
thus, all those worlds, anointed with that merit, will possess auspicious faculties.
"Having enjoyed excellent glory and true happiness, they will at the end go to the abode of the Jinas"—
this and more was heard as it was prophesied by the Lord of Sages, Vipaśyin.
"All the people gathered in the assembly rejoiced, having been awakened.
Thus did I hear the instruction given by the Teacher Vipaśyin.
"Thus, for the sake of awakening you, it has been fully explained;
let it be understood," so was it commanded by the Lord of Sages, Śrīghana—this is what is heard.
Maitreya and all the others who were present beheld him and were completely filled with serene joy.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Origin of the Self-Arisen Dharmadhātu.
The second chapter is named "The Description of the Fruit of Worship."
Then the wise Mahāsattva Maitreya, that son of the Victor, having bowed again to the Blessed One with palms joined, spoke thus: (Svayambhūpurāṇa 2.1)
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the excellent narrative concerning the origin of the Self-Existent;
may you relate it for the sake of awakening the worlds.
When this had been thus requested by the wise Maitreya, the Blessed One, looking toward those people in the assembly, gave this instruction: *Svayambhū Purāṇa* 2.3.
"Excellent, Maitreya! May all those present in this assembly listen with respect;
I shall fully proclaim the noble narrative of the self-arisen origin."
For example, when the Lord of Sages, Vipaśyin, had passed into nirvāṇa,
after a long interval of time, there appeared here once again a teacher of the world.
The Lord of Sages named Śikhin was an Arhat, a Tathāgata, a King of Dharma,
the Omniscient One, a Sugata, the Sovereign of all sciences, and a Guide.
At that time, when the lifespan of humans was seventy thousand years,
I was indeed a Bodhisattva named Kṣemaṅkara.
When that Blessed One, the Teacher, the Lord of the Śikhin-dharma, the Victor,
was dwelling in the hermitage of the Sugata on the outskirts of the city named Aruṇā.
Then all the great beings, the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Victors,
attended upon and served that Teacher Śikhin;
I too likewise [served] him, Śikhin, the teacher of the three worlds.
Having approached for refuge, I always worshipped him with joy;
on one occasion there, that Arhat, the Blessed One, the Omniscient One, the Crest-jewel [of the Śākya clan], [was present].
In order to teach the true Dharma, he should take his seat upon the assembly-throne;
seeing this, all the monks, disciples, and those practicing the holy life [should likewise do so].
The bhikṣus, all those observing vows, the upāsakas, and the upāsikās,
having approached that Sage in order to drink the nectar of his true Dharma, [gathered around him].
Having bowed there with palms joined and circumambulated, one should take refuge;
at that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Gods, and all the deities arrived.
All the lords of the world have also assembled to hear the Dharma,
as well as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Sādhyas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras.
The Garuḍas, the lords of the Rākṣasas, the Daityas, and even the sovereigns of the Nāgas;
the Ṛṣis and the Brāhmaṇas, as well as the Tīrthikas and the ascetics.
Ascetics, yogins, and also the Nirgranthas and Digambaras;
kings, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, and common people.
Artisans, merchants, caravan leaders, and other great men;
citizens, country-dwellers, villagers, as well as those residing in other lands.
Filled with joy to drink that nectar of the True Dharma, they gathered there;
having arrived and beheld that Lord of Sages, they stood before him.
Having worshipped them in due order and performed circumambulations,
having joined his palms in reverence and bowed down, he turned around in every direction.
Having placed them at his front, gazed upon them, and approached them with great respect,
the Blessed Lord Śikhin saw all of them seated together.
He perfectly taught the True Dharma, which is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end;
having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all the worlds were awakened.
At that very time, in that lake which was a reservoir of merit, they became partakers of enlightenment, being intent upon accomplishing the true Dharma.
It had a jeweled stalk, with great brilliance and diamond filaments;
it was the pericarp of a divine king of lotuses, composed of the five precious gems.
A great lotus appeared, shining with a thousand petals;
in the central circle of the pericarp of that jewel-lotus, [he arose].
Self-arisen and spontaneously manifest, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is the abode of the Victors;
it is one cubit in measure, radiant and composed of pure jewels.
The support of the qualities of the glory of perfect enlightenment, adorned with all the primary marks,
having the nature of light, the eldest in the world, and the refuge of the five Tathāgatas.
The Lord of the world, adored by the world, worshiped by the world, the Sovereign of the world;
without beginning or end, undecaying, venerable, and the bearer of all auspicious purposes. (Svayambhū Purāṇa 2.27)
He is the foremost and most excellent form of Samantabhadra, the bearer of the jewel of the True Dharma;
he is the sovereign lord of the virtuous qualities of the three worlds and the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life.
And when that caitya had arisen, the oceans, mountains, and the earth trembled.
Divine, fragrant flowers fell from the abode of the gods;
celestial drums resounded, and all the directions became serene.
The fires turned to the right, auspicious in appearance and free from flickering;
the winds blew steadily, cool, fragrant, and pleasant. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 2.31)
Clouds with deep rumbling sounds rained down waters of divine flavor;
the planets, stars, and moon shone forth, illuminating the assembly hall.
In the sky, the sounds of hymns, auspicious chants,
and songs resounded everywhere with constant and great enthusiasm for supreme auspiciousness.

Abundance of food, the manifestation of glorious virtues, the practice of the true Dharma, and the accomplishment of auspicious deeds— free from calamity and characterized by virtuous conduct— prevailed everywhere.
Having thus beheld that very self-arisen Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Victors, all [the gods] beginning with Īśa, who reside in the formless realms, [approached].
Even amidst the bliss of the great joy of yogic meditation,
they ceased their festivities and proceeded to pay homage to that self-existent Lord.
Likewise, all the sages beginning with Brahmā, being celibate practitioners,
approached with joy to behold the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū).
Thus Śakra and all the other gods of the Thirty-three, together with their hosts of Apsarases,
joyfully went to see him, taking with them the various articles for worship.
Likewise, Agni, Dharmarāja, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Marut, Śrīda, and Bhūtādhipa— all these lords of the worlds as well— [are situated there].
Together with their respective retinues, filled with great enthusiasm and joy,
they thus approached to behold the Svayambhū Caitya.
The great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, rejoicing with the Gandharvas,
came together with them to see him, through their enthusiasm for singing and instrumental music.
King Virūḍhaka, together with the Kumbhāṇḍas,
joyfully approached to pay homage to the Self-Existent One upon seeing him.
Virūpākṣa also, together with all the lords of the nāgas and the rulers of the serpent race,
came to behold him, bearing offerings of jewels and worship.
Kuvera, the king of the yakṣas, accompanied by yakṣiṇīs,
also came to see him, bearing various offerings of material goods.
And Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, accompanied by all the Guhyakas,
arrived to see him, carrying away their divine enjoyments.
Druma, the king of the kinnaras, together with all his followers and with the joyful sounds of various musical instruments, came to see the Blessed One.
Likewise, the lord of all the Vidyādharas, named Sarvārthasiddha,
came to see him, bearing divine offerings for worship.
Even Garuḍa, the king of birds, together with all the hosts of birds,
came to behold him, accompanied by the great splendor and enthusiasm of their respective supernatural powers.
Thus, both the Siddhas and the Sādhyas, the Vasus and the planets as well,
all the star-women and all the hosts of Apsarases [are present].
Thus all the lords of the Daityas, together with their respective retinues and accompanied by great abundance and power, suddenly approached him.
Thus all the lords of the world, situated in the ten directions,
having seen him who was self-arisen, proceeded swiftly to pay him homage.
All of them, having gathered together and beheld that Lord of the World,
their hearts filled with joy, bowed from afar and approached him.
Then, O Lord of the World, they all, having worshipped him in due order and performed prostration with the eight limbs, paid their respects with great devotion.
Some joyfully worshipped him by anointing him with fragrant substances;
some with various kinds of flowers, and others with enchanting incenses.
Some [honored him] with garlands of flowers, some with divine robes,
some with rows of lamps, and some with offerings of incense.
Some [were honored] with divine nectars for enjoyment, some with divine medicinal herbs,
and some with various kinds of divine jewel ornaments and decorations.
Some [honored him] with parasols, banners, yak-tail whisks, and canopies;
others with musical performances accompanied by mṛdaṅgas, murajas, and other instruments.
Some [played] with the triple symphony (tauryatrika), some with flutes, conchs, and horns;
others likewise with kahanas, and still others with stringed instruments such as the vīṇā.

With thick percussion instruments such as the *tāla* and others, with kettledrums (*bherī*), *ānaka*, and *mardala* drums, as well as various kinds of *maḍḍuka*, *ḍiṇḍima*, *jharjhara*, and so forth; SvayambhuP_2.59.
Some with dances and songs, and some with cries of "Hāhā," they worshipped that temple of the Jina with such various kinds of enthusiasm.
Some, by the thousands, paid homage by performing circumambulations alone;
others did so with joy through the recitation of dhāraṇīs, vidyās, praises, and other such acts.
Thus, all those worlds, beginning with the twice-born, having taken refuge in him with faith, worshipped that Self-Existent One in various ways.
Having heard this account, which had been set forth with divine and great enthusiasm, all those present in the assembly were filled with wonder.
Having observed that, the Great Being Ratnapāṇi, standing before him,
bowed to the sage Śikhin with palms joined in reverence and spoke thus:
O Blessed One, for what reason has this entire earth trembled and this divine festival been proclaimed? Please explain the cause of this.
When this had been thus prayed for by that wise Ratnapāṇi,
the Blessed One Śikhin, beholding him, spoke to that Ratnapāṇi.
"Listen well, O Great Being! The reason why the entire earth has trembled and why divine splendors have manifested is now being declared."
For example, here on this earth, in the Himalayas to the north,
there is a lake that is a reservoir of meritorious waters endowed with the eightfold qualities.
There, upon the pericarp of a lotus made of jewels— the sovereign of blossoms—
the Abode of the Victors, the Dharmadhātu, arose spontaneously of itself.
When that was produced, the entire earth was fashioned and filled with great joy;
everywhere in the abode of existence, auspicious enthusiasm began to prevail.
Beholding him, Maheśāna, Brahmā, Śakra, and the other immortals— the planets, the stars, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, and even the Vidyādharas— [were struck with wonder].
And all the great seers were filled with wonder and joy;
likewise, all the lords of the worlds, the Daityas, the Nāgas, and the lords of the birds [were moved].
The yakṣas, kinnaras, gandharvas, guhyakas, and rākṣasas—
all these and others likewise— beheld that Self-Existent One.
Filled with joy, they gather together and celebrate with great festivals;
thus, the great enthusiasm for this worship has been fully set in motion.
"This great portent has arisen for this reason," so was it instructed by the Lord of Sages, Śikhin; and having heard this, he [the king] was filled with deep reflection.
The great beings, the Jewel-in-Hand, were filled with wonder and joy;
their lotus-faces were fully awakened, and their intentions were greatly gladdened.
Bowing once more to Śikhin with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus:
"O Blessed One, please understand that which my mind desires."
Having granted permission for that, he should please [him] here.
I too [sought refuge] in that Lord, the Self-Existent One, the Teacher of the World.
Relying upon him with faith, I worship him with great festivals.
When he had thus prayed, the Blessed One Śikhin heard him.
Beholding the Great Being Ratnapāṇi, he gave this instruction:
"Noble son, proceed quickly if you desire awakening."
Having taken refuge with faith, worship that abode of the Jina;
those who take refuge there shall worship it with faith and joy.
"Having swiftly attained perfect awakening, may they reach the state of a fully enlightened Buddha"—
having heard this and other such instructions from the Lord of Sages, Ratnapāṇi [acted accordingly].
Having bowed to that sage with palms joined in reverence, he then proceeded joyfully;
thereafter, many bodhisattvas, sons of the Conquerors, accompanied him.
There were also disciples— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
who were full of devotion, observant of their vows, and longing for merit.
Sages and Brahmins as well, ascetics and yogis too, heretics and forest-dwellers, the Nirgranthas and those practicing celibacy; SvayambhuP_2.85.
Kings, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, and common people;
artisans, merchants, caravan leaders, and great men as well.
The citizens, the country folk, the villagers, as well as those dwelling in other lands—
likewise all other people who desire the virtues of the true Dharma.
There, all of them moved joyfully with him in great enthusiasm;
thus Ratnapāṇi was accompanied by all those people.
Taking up the components of worship, he performed them with great enthusiasm and joy;
thus did that illustrious and preeminent one bring delight to all the worlds.
Arriving there suddenly, he beheld this temple of the Jina;
seeing it, that Great Being approached with joy.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites and having prostrated, they all— those great sages who were his companions— honored him with joy.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites, they venerated [him] with great enthusiasm and joy;
thus all those people, having offered praise and recited the dhāraṇī, [departed]. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 2.92)
Having performed circumambulations and prostrated eight times, they worshipped with joy;
so too did other great beings, the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Jinas.
Having assembled from the ten directions, they took possession of this Lord;
at that time, I too went along with him, Ratnapāṇi.
Having taken refuge with faith in this Lord Prābhāji,
by the power of this merit, may they attain enlightenment even in this degenerate age.
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra, I shall become the sovereign of the Dharma.
Whosoever, relying upon whichever [deity], should worship with faith and joy.
May they all, having attained perfect enlightenment, quickly become Sugatas.
Thus, the merit arising from such service is exceedingly great.
"Possessing the excellent qualities of auspicious glory, it is the means for accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
thus has it been proclaimed on all sides by all the Lords of Sages."
You too, having fully understood this, should worship it with great reverence;
for even all the Lords of Munis [worship it] four times during the day and night.
Having seen him, having meditated upon him, and having maintained mindfulness,
all the Buddhas currently residing in every direction worship him with great reverence.
And all those yet to come shall likewise always honor him;
by the mere sight of him, even the wicked and sinful are purified.
For they shall quickly be freed from their transgressions and possess stainless faculties;
thereafter, being pure in soul, free from afflictions, and celibate practitioners, they shall abide.
They shall never, at any time, go to any state of woe whatsoever.
United together from their very birth, they were the abodes of auspicious glory and excellent virtues.
May they become Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, sons of the Sugata;
then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order, [they shall attain it].
"Having attained the threefold enlightenment, may they reach the state of nirvāṇa.
Having thus bowed down and always gazed upon him with reverence, [one should proceed]. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 2.105)
Those who desire awakening should always rejoice in [merit], recollect it, meditate upon it, and experience its power;
they should even utter the name [of the Tathāgata] with faith.
"Devotional service should always be performed with respect according to one's capacity"—
this and more was thus instructed by the Lord of Sages, Śrīghana, as it is heard.
All the members of the assembly, headed by Maitreya, were awakened;
they gave their assent, saying "So be it," to the Self-Existent One regarding the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Then all those present in the assembly desired to worship with devotion, taking refuge in the Self-Existent One, the Dharmadhātu.
Desiring once more to hear the specific fruits of worship,
the Great Being Maitreya, the son of the Sugata, reflected upon that.
Bowing thus, he made this request to the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages:
"O Blessed One, [please explain] the detailed expansion of the specific fruits of this worship."
All these members of the assembly now desire to hear;
therefore, may the Blessed One explain the specific excellence of the fruit of worship.
"May he be able to awaken all those seated in this assembly"—
having heard this request made by Maitreya, he [the Lord]...
Beholding those people in the assembly, the Blessed One instructed them thus:
"Listen, all you people, to the great fruit of this worship."
I shall explain in detail for the enlightenment of all the worlds [the rite] with the five nectars together with waters that are beautifully adorned and perfectly pure.
Those who joyfully bathe this Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Jinas, have always bathed in the Mandākinī; they are pure in the three spheres.
Experiencing divine pleasures at the edge where the abodes of the Victors are located,
and where there are self-arisen shrines (caityas) endowed with fragrant substances.
Always gladdening the minds of the world, they joyfully incense the virtuous;
with their fragrant and gentle limbs, those gods are honored even by the asuras.
In that abode of the Jinas, the Dharmadhātu, they become glorious, endowed with excellent voices, and like jewels, joyfully perfumed by the five fragrances.
Having worshipped Liptā and taken refuge [in her], they always revere her with devotion;
endowed with the seven jewels, they become the abode of auspicious glory and excellent virtues.
All the lords of the earth become intent upon the welfare of the world,
as do the sovereign kings of sages here, adorned with variegated robes and garments.
Having been invited, they worship with faith and devotion, full of respect.
They were adorned with divine silks and ornaments of precious gems.
Those who possess mastery over the Dharma become wise and practitioners of auspicious conduct;
and those who honor this [Buddha] with all kinds of flowers, both aquatic and terrestrial, [attain the same].
Having honored and taken refuge [in them], they enjoy [them] with great joy;
endowed with the prosperity and glory of lords of the earth, they possess a radiance exceeding that of Śakra.
Those who adorn this [stūpa] with beautiful, enchanting garlands of flowers become endowed with auspicious glory and happiness, and partakers of enlightenment.
Having adorned [the shrine] with all kinds of flowers and hanging garlands, they worship;
those who desire the Dharma become lords of the gods, endowed with glory and prosperity.
Those of good reputation, who are devoted to virtues, auspicious, and practicing the conduct of awakening, who joyfully offer all flowers here in the abode of the Sugata; ||| SvayambhuP_2.127 |||
Having scattered [offerings] and propitiated [the deity], those who take refuge and devote themselves to him—
whether they be lords of the gods gone to heaven or lords of men upon the earth— [attain their goals].
Those endowed with great and glorious virtues become partakers of enlightenment,
having offered lamps that dispel darkness, fueled by fragrant oils and the like, and brightly blazing.
Those who, though appearing very fierce, are in fact beautiful, joyfully kindle the lamp of wisdom that dispels the darkness within this realm of phenomena, the abode of the Victors.
Those whose lotus-feet are worshipped by kings become partakers of enlightenment;
they enjoy exquisite food fit for the gods, endowed with excellent fragrance.
And those lords of men who, having approached him, worship him with devotion, become possessed of supernatural powers and endowed with the seven jewels.
Even those who partake of the divine drink,
endowed with a golden fragrance, in this world become lords of the gods in heaven and partakers of enlightenment.
Having presented offerings and propitiated [the deity],
those who worship with concentrated minds become the most powerful lords of the earth, endowed with prosperity and free from disease.
And those lords of the gods who have gone to heaven become partakers of enlightenment,
as do those who [plant] roots, seeds, leaves, and fruits at the base of this self-arisen tree.
Having established [the deity] with faith, those who have taken refuge worship him;
they enjoy various objects of pleasure according to their desire, as if they were lords.
Those who are devoted to the practice of the true Dharma go at the end to the abode of the Victors;
and those who, within this support of the Sugata, [apply] even collections of wholesome medicines.
Those who are constantly offered with faith and served with great respect become most powerful,
with well-nourished limbs, gentle senses, and free from disease.
Having enjoyed the happiness of royal splendor, he goes at the end to Sukhāvatī;
and those who [dwell] here in this self-arisen Dharmadhātu, the support of the Jinas.
And having spread out a lofty canopy, they were attended with great respect.
Blessed are they—virtuous, worthy of veneration, of pure lineage, and discerning.
Those who, in this abode of the Sugata, [erect] various lofty banners, shall attain the fulfillment of all goals and go at last to the abode of the Jina.
Having planted [the seeds of merit] with great enthusiasm, they are honored and rejoice;
becoming streams of the bliss of auspicious and excellent virtues, they become sovereign lords of the earth on this world.
In heaven, the lords of the gods eventually proceed to the abode of the Jinas—
those who offered various parasols made of gold, jewels, flowers, and other such things.
Having ascended here with great enthusiasm, those lords of men and lords of gods, being filled with joy, shall always enjoy themselves like parasols throughout existence.
Having enjoyed great pleasures, those who [erect] five-colored banners in this abode of the Sugata go at the end to the dwelling place of the Jina.
Even though they have attained equality, they shall rejoice in great festivals;
having become rulers of the earth here, they will always be even the lords of the gods.
Having enjoyed excellent glory and true happiness, those who perform musical concerts with various instruments such as drums and the like in this place go at the end to the abode of the Jinas.
They are also attended by great festivals featuring music, flutes, and other instruments;
they are the abode of divine splendor, auspiciousness, and excellent virtues, possessing enchanting sounds.
Having performed the practice of the True Dharma, they go to the abode of the Sugata;
and those who offer parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers in this abode of the Sugata [attain the same].
Having cast [the seed] with faith and devotion, they worship with great respect;
they do not go to an evil rebirth, but are always born in a state of union.
Having brought benefit to all sentient beings, they proceed to the abode of the Victors,
where those who joyfully offer reliquaries, substances, jewels, and so forth, receive their reward.
Having offered with faith, they always enjoy themselves with great respect;
partaking in divine splendor and happiness, they are the refuge of auspicious glory and virtuous qualities.
Having brought about the welfare of all sentient beings, they proceed to the abode of the Victors;
and those who, with joy, [praise] this abode of the Buddhas with truthful hymns of praise.
Having praised [the deity] with both verses and prose, they worship with devotion;
enriched with many jewels, they are experts in all branches of knowledge.
Even kings and lords of heaven, having become such, in the end go to the state of the Sugata;
therefore, with faith, take refuge in this Self-Existent One, the Lord of the World.
Those who, having bowed with the eight limbs of prostration, worship [the deity] with devotion and respect,
become lords of kings endowed with the seven jewels and possessed of great supernatural powers.
Those who practice the conduct of awakening become devoted to accomplishing the True Dharma,
and they perform circumambulations many times around this king of shrines.
Having performed [the rite], meditated, recollected, and even having uttered the name while worshipping,
they become rememberers of past lives, long-lived, wise, and possessed of beautiful complexions.
Those who practice for awakening (bodhicārin) shall be worthy of salutation, worship, and honor;
they shall be pure, having been smeared all over with ashes as a cleansing agent.
Those who, with great enthusiasm, worship this Lord after having honored him well,
become long-lived and are freed from the torment of the fires of grief and affliction.
May those kings who have removed the faded flower offerings (nirmālya) and purified this place on all sides become free from disease and happy.
Relying upon this [teaching], those whose minds are devoted to the Perfectly Awakened One cultivate it;

Having established [the image], they worship it with great enthusiasm and deep respect;
endowed with all prosperity, their faculties are fully developed and free from disease.
Desiring the Dharma and practicing virtue, they shall become practitioners of awakening,
having recited his mantras and dhāraṇīs with a concentrated mind.
Having meditated, recollected, and even uttered the name,
all those great beings (mahāsattvas) possess the complete purity of the three spheres.
May those who practice for awakening become bearers of auspicious glory and excellent virtues;
such is the exceedingly great merit in this protection of the Dharma.

now, however, I shall describe it in brief according to my own merit. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 2.168)

thus one should consider that the fruit of honor and worship for this [text] is exceedingly great.

Toward the Tathāgatas and also toward the disciples of the perfectly awakened ones who uphold the true Dharma.

"Venerable One, I wish to hear that discourse on the stages;
may you correctly instruct us and awaken us to it."

"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my Guru;

Teaching all of that, he awakened us all. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 3.7)

The King of Dharma, Lord of Sages, Arhat, Tathāgata, Guide,

the Pratyekabuddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and even the naked ascetics [were moved].
Bhikṣuṇīs, celibate practitioners, and those striving who are yet unyoked,

Having joyfully honored and bowed in due order to the Lord of Sages with palms joined in reverence, in order to drink that nectar of the True Dharma, [he approached] with devotion.

Śakra and the others, as well as the lords of all the worlds,

Having all come together with the Sāgas, they honored and bowed to the Blessed One in due order, and then took their seats in the assembly.
And thus, O wise ones, there were Brahmins, as well as Kṣatriya kings,
