Artisans and merchants, caravan leaders and citizens,
as well as villagers, country folk, and other inhabitants of the land.
Having all approached the Blessed One in due order, they honored him, bowed down, and also performed circumambulations.
Placing their teacher at the forefront and surrounding him on all sides,
they stood with concentrated minds to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Seeing them seated together, the Blessed One, the Victorious One, Viśvabhū,
taught the True Dharma, which is auspicious in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all those present in the assembly,
having understood the excellence of the Dharma, attained joy and were awakened.
At that moment, the entire earth, along with its mountains and forests, became serene;
all the quarters shone brightly like the sun, the moon, and fire.
Divine drums resounded and showers of flowers fell;
free from any portents, a great enthusiasm prevailed on all sides.
Beholding that, all those people in the assembly were filled with wonder;
looking up at the Omniscient One, they stood there eager to hear the reason for it.
Then the Bodhisattva named Gaganagañja arose,
wearing his upper robe over one shoulder and standing respectfully before him.

Having bowed with palms joined in reverence to that omniscient one, the great possessor of supernormal knowledges, the King of Dharma, the Guide, the Sage Viśvabhū, he spoke thus: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 3.33.
"O Blessed One, for whom does this desire to see you arise now? May you, O Guru, instruct us and enlighten us regarding that."
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
looked toward Gaganagañja and spoke thus to the assembly:
"Noble son, this great and auspicious omen has appeared;
therefore, I shall explain it to you. Listen with reverence! (Svayambhūpurāṇa 3.36)
For example, Mañjuśrī, the son of the Sugata, who possesses the threefold supernatural knowledges,
dwells in a mountain hermitage in Mahācīna in the north.
His two wives were Keśinī, the elder,
who was the bestower of fortune and endowed with knowledge and excellent virtues, and the second, Upakeśinī.
At one time, there, Mañjuśrī, that ocean of virtuous qualities,
joyfully entered the meditative absorption named "Manifestation of the World."
Beholding [the world] through meditative absorption, he saw there, within a lotus of a great lake,
the Dharmadhātu— the abode of the Victors— spontaneously arisen as composed of jewels.
Beholding that Self-Existent One, Mañjudeva, Susanmati was filled with joy; reflecting further, he thought thus within his mind: *Svayambhuva Purāṇa* 3.41.
Aha! The self-arisen Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Victors, stands in this solitary watery place in the form of light, speaking.
Therefore, having gone there to that great lake, I shall act in such a way as to dry up its waters so that it becomes the surface of the earth.
Then, upon that mountain peak which is well-established, waterless, and firm,
having installed him there, I shall worship that Lord.
Likewise, when it has become the earth there, its dwelling place shall be villages and so forth;
then all the people of this world shall resort to that abode of the Jina.
Likewise, through the power of that merit, there shall always be auspiciousness therein;
indeed, it shall be free from calamities, and the people shall be of virtuous character.
Then all those humans, having taken refuge in him alone,
should always worship him with great enthusiasm and joy according to their ability.
Then those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, purified by that merit and longing for the qualities of the True Dharma, should practice the vow of awakening.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order and having attained the threefold method, they shall reach the state of cessation.
Having thus performed this great merit and attained it throughout the three worlds,
and having established the Dharma, may I attain enlightenment and reach the state of final liberation.
Having thus meditated and reached a firm decision, Mañjuśrī, the son of the Victorious One,
possessing great supernatural power, assumed the form of the master known as Mañjudeva.
The one named Keśinī was called Varadā, while the one known as Mokṣadā became Akeśinī;
having become thus, she practiced with many great beings along with all of them.
Then Mañjuśrī, together with his wife and his followers,
traveled everywhere, conducting himself with great magnificence while maintaining a state of benevolence toward all.
Having approached there from afar, they beheld that abode of the Jina, brilliantly radiant, situated in the midst of a great lake lotus.
There, having beheld that blazing form of light,
they bowed down, approached him suddenly, and performed circumambulations.
All of them took refuge on that delightful mountain on its shore;
beholding that very shrine, they dwelt there filled with joy.
Then, having risen at dawn, the powerful Mañjuśrī,
with supreme devotion, himself praised the self-arisen Jina-abode.
Salutation to You who are the form of light, whose nature is consciousness,
who are without beginning or end, the bestower of prosperity, and whose form is the Praṇava.
Salutation with *svāhā* to the one whose form faces all directions, who has the nature of *svadhā*,
the creator of the elements such as earth, and whose essential nature is great splendor.
Salutations again and again to the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the supporter of the world;
salutations to you who are worthy of the world’s veneration and the supreme object of the world’s worship.
Salutations to You, who are both exceedingly gross and subtle, the transformation and the transformer,
the formless creator, whose very embodiment is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Salutations to you, the consumer of oblations, who are yourself the very essence of the *vaṣaṭ* call;
salutations to you, the priest (*hotṛ*) whose form is the invocation, and to you, the sacrificial substance itself.
Salutations to you, who are attainable through devotion, who are gentle, and who are affectionate toward your devotees;
salutations to you, who are accessible through meditation, who are the object of meditation, and who bestow the fourfold aims of human life.
Constant salutation to the supreme jewel, whose majesty is limitless;
constant salutation to Yoga, which transcends all qualities, and to the Yogin.
Having praised him thus, Mañjuśrī again sought forgiveness:
"Be gracious, O Blessed One, for I strove to dry up this lake."
Having spoken thus, he prepared his sword Candrahāsa and,
after circumambulating [it] three times, looked all around.
Having observed that the mountain was covered by the southern direction,
that Great Being cut through the water-reservoir with his sword, Candrahāsa, and created a lake.
Having quickly emerged on all sides through the path of the split mountain, all those waters reached their confluence with the Gaṅgā.
From that time forth, rivers and streams appeared upon the earth;
the cardinal and intermediate directions were filled with waters of impurity, along with the islands.
There, having cut all the living beings that have perished in the water or those that dwell upon the rocks, he should cause them to roam in their own respective places.
Having thus cut it through on all sides and made an outlet for that water,
he would not have drained all the waters even in three nights.
He established a single water-holding lake named Dhanada-hrada,
which served as the hermitage for the nāga Karkoṭaka.
When they were attacked by a lion, O Lord of Elephants, overwhelmed with fear,
they fled in the ten directions, crying out with loud shrieks.
Thus, that mass of water emerged from another path through the cutting of the Candrahāsa sword, leaving behind only mud, as it were.
Then, at that very time, he established a lake named Dharādraha as a reservoir for water,
providing a dwelling place for the nāga Karkoṭaka.
Then, when that water had dried up,
the very lotus that was his support became a mountain and remained as the locus of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Through the power of Mañjudeva, that mountain, which was spoken of as being composed of all [other] mountains,
became indivisible by Vajravaktra and is known as Vajrakūṭa.
Then that delightful region on the surface of the earth, surrounded on all sides by mountains, is called Upachandoha; it is also said to be Himālaya.
The wisdom that is difficult to conquer, whose nature is the ground of being, and which brings about the experience of primordial gnosis,
abides having assumed the form of the Heruka maṇḍala.
And there too, the principal one is the illustrious Mahādevī Khagānanā;
having arisen from the source of Dharma, she abides for the welfare of the world.
Upon seeing him, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrīdeva, of great conduct and great supernatural power,
was filled with joy.
Then, beholding that Great Goddess, he was filled with joy;
[he honored her] with his chest, his head, his gaze, his speech, and likewise his mind.
It is recorded as being "eight-limbed" (aṣṭāṅga) because it involves the two feet, the two hands, and the two knees;
having performed this prostration with eight limbs, one should remain with palms joined in reverence.
With his lotus-face exceedingly serene and his lotus-eyes fully awakened,
he gazed upon that Great Goddess and thus worshipped her with joy through hymns of praise.
O Blessed Great Goddess, I go for refuge to you;
I constantly revere your lotus feet—may she be pleased with me.
You alone are the mother of all Buddhas, the bestower of enlightenment;
you are the mother of all Bodhisattvas, who protects their welfare.
She bestows the enjoyment of the welfare of all, purifies all sins,
unshakably subdues the hosts of wicked Māras, and grants the bliss of great joy.
She bestows the qualities of enthusiasm, strength, and vigor for accomplishing the True Dharma;
she grants the bliss of meditative absorption and concentration that is free from afflictions and utterly tranquil.
The great jewel of the qualities of wisdom, which bestows glorious prosperity—
I, taking refuge at her lotus feet through devotion to her, worship her.
Having thus made this earnest prayer, that wise Mañjuśrī, who was Samvara,
with a mind purified by devotion toward her, desired to propitiate her.
Then, on the ninth day of the fortnight, a Sunday, that preceptor, together with his retinue, was filled with joy there on the summit of the mountain path.
Having bathed in the morning, his soul purified and clad in clean garments, the wise one,
having undertaken the poṣadha vows, remained there worshipping the Goddess.
Having kept vigil throughout the night, they propitiated the Sovereign of Jinas by reciting the dhāraṇīs and mantras, and by offering hymns of praise.
Then, on the tenth day at dawn, having bathed with perfumed water with joy and having given gifts according to his desire, he was purified in the three spheres.
Having worshipped that goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, according to the prescribed rite,
and having offered praise with great fervor, he performed three circumambulations.

With his lotus-face exceedingly serene and his mind intent upon the virtues of the True Dharma, he should again bow with the eight limbs and, with palms joined in the *añjali* mudrā, make this request: SvayambhuP_3.96.
O Mother of the World, may you be gracious to me who has taken refuge in you;
with joy, I shall always worship you, who are eager to accomplish perfect enlightenment.
Having thus prayed and bowed with joy using the eight-limbed prostration,
those two who are fully wise should take that nectar from her lotus-foot with the three-fingered gesture and drink it.
Having drunk that nectar, he— purified in the three spheres and liberated from the eight inopportune states— attained the moment of perfect enlightenment.
Having acted thus, that teacher, devoted to the Goddess,
attained the moment of perfect enlightenment and became the sovereign of all phenomena.
Then that glorious master, the Bodhisattva devoted to the welfare of the world,
dwelt there with his assemblies in hermitages that were forms of the dharmadhātu.
Because it was consecrated by him, that place became known everywhere as the glorious and enchanting Mañjuśrīparvata.
Always relying there upon this very dharmadhātu,
that son of the Jina, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, applied himself with devotion.
All those pure observers, headed by Brahmā and Indra,
as well as all the lords of the worlds, gathered there with joy.
Having observed the poṣadha right there and having kept a vigil during the night,
one should dwell [there] while reciting the dhāraṇī-mantra and meditating upon that glorious Jineśvarī.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite and performed circumambulations, and having prostrated with the eight limbs, he joyfully honored him with hymns of praise. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 3.106)
Thus, all those who had taken refuge in that Great Goddess attained the perfection of the qualities of Dharmaśrī, as well as great supernatural power and spiritual accomplishment.
Then all those immortals, including Indra, Brahmā, and the other lords,
gazed upon that mountain peak Vajrakūṭa, the lotus-like abode of the Jinas.
Having rejoiced and welcomed [the teachings], they too have gone for refuge;
having honored them with great enthusiasm, they devote themselves with deep respect.
Then all those immortals and all those lords of the worlds [honored] this very Mañjudeva, the Vajrācārya, the true guru.
Having approached the sanctuary and worshipped with divine offerings and great enthusiasm,
they paid homage, filled with joy.
In this way, Manu and all others— the Manus, the great seers (maharṣis),
ascetics, yogins, monks, and celibate students— [attained their status].
The Cailaka Bodhisattvas and Mahāsattvas, the sons of the Victors,
all approached that goddess as her lay disciples.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites, they offered their devotion with great joy;
thereafter, they all took refuge in the Dharmadhātu.
Having worshipped with great enthusiasm, having bowed and performed circumambulations,
his lotus-like face became serene and his heart was filled with joy.
Then those great beings, filled with joy, honored the teacher Mañjuśrī, who possesses great supernatural power, with their enthusiastic efforts.
All the Pratyekabuddhas and Sugatas also gathered there;
she honored that Goddess Dharmadhātu and the Teacher.
And all the Tathāgatas, too, by means of the emission of clouds of offerings,
worship that Goddess Dharmadhātu, that Ācārya, and that Samācārya.
Other people as well, having become corrupted in such a manner,
arrived there and devoted themselves to that goddess, the Dharmadhātu, and to that teacher.
By the power of this merit, the earth, including its oceans and mountains, has trembled;
a rain of flowers proceeds from all sides with auspicious vigor.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū perceived them;
all the worlds took refuge [in him] and were filled with wonder.
Then all those worlds also desired to behold that goddess Śrī Maheśvarī, the supreme teacher of the dharmadhātu.
Having fully understood his intention, Gaganagañja rose up; beholding the Blessed One with a focused mind, he spoke thus: Svayambhūpurāṇa 3.123.
O Blessed One, all desire to behold that Sovereign Lady of Sugatas, the Dharmadhātu, and that Teacher; therefore, grant us your permission.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, looking upon that self-knower Gaganagañja, gave this instruction: Svayambhūpurāṇa 3.125.
If you wish to see the great goddess Sādhyā, Khagānanā, and Jineśvarī, as well as that Ācārya Dharmadhātu, then do so! Svayambhū Purāṇa 3.126.
Having gone there to the Himālaya, worship that Śrī Devī Khagānanā and that Ācārya Dharmadhātu according to the prescribed ritual.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
all the people, filled with great enthusiasm and rejoicing, went forth that very night.
I too, having received the permission of the Lord of Sages, set out joyfully with them; seeing him from afar, I approached.
Having joyfully beheld this realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) here, I attained it;
having honored it with great enthusiasm, I rejoiced together with those beings.
Having gone for refuge with faith, having circumambulated him,
having praised him with the eight limbs [of prostration], and having bowed down, one should pray for the vow of awakening (bodhisamvara).
Then, having beheld that teacher named Mañjudeva and having honored him with great enthusiasm, you, along with your younger brothers, took refuge in him.
Then, having propitiated that Śrī Devī Khagānanā according to the prescribed rites through her instructions, I worshipped her with great fervor.
Having performed circumambulation and prostrated with the eight limbs, filled with joy,
and having praised and meditated upon perfect enlightenment, he prayed for the welfare of the world.
By the power of this merit, with the three spheres completely purified,
the Bodhisattva becomes accomplished, liberated from the eight inopportune states.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order and having conquered the hosts of Māra, he becomes an Arhat and even a Victor (Jina) in the Kali age.
Thus, those who have taken refuge in this Great Goddess should worship her according to the prescribed rites and, with minds set on awakening, devote themselves to her.
All those great beings shall have the three spheres completely purified;
they shall be Bodhisattvas possessing the great superknowledges, lords of the three qualities.
May they never go anywhere to an evil rebirth,
and may they always be born in association with those who are the refuge of glorious virtues.
Having respectfully given whatever substance is desired to those who seek it,
and having enjoyed happiness according to their wishes, one should move about for the welfare of the world.
Then, possessing pure ethical discipline and abiding in the four divine abodes,
they should always practice what is virtuous, having undertaken the bodhisattva vow.
Then they shall become great beings, longing for the bliss of the true Dharma,
devoted to the vow of patience that protects and maintains the welfare of both themselves and others.
Then those who are the repositories of the six virtues, heroic and discerning,
being intent upon accomplishing the true Dharma, shall become lords of the three qualities.
Then those wise and steadfast ones, free from afflictions and having conquered their senses,
endowed with the qualities of meditative concentration, shall become yogins of enlightenment.
Then those sons of the Sugata, pure in soul, masters of all sciences and virtues, shall attain the jewel of the glory of wisdom.
And thereafter, all those beings, eager for the welfare of all sentient beings and wise regarding the methods for [overcoming] all miserable states, may they become lords of the three qualities.
Then, those oceans of jewels of aspirations for the equipment of enlightenment,
having brought about the welfare of all sentient beings, shall always proceed toward what is auspicious.
And then those who possess great supernormal knowledges, endowed with auspicious glory and true virtues,
being most powerful and conquerors of the wicked, shall become lords of the three worlds.
Then, having attained the threefold enlightenment, those practitioners of the auspicious conduct shall become lords of sages, perfected in the supreme essence of the wisdom of perfect awakening.
Then those Sugatas, the Buddhas, the Victors who are lords of the ten stages,
having established all beings on the path to enlightenment, would make them all practitioners of the sublime Dharma.
Having thus made [themselves] composed of Dharma throughout all worlds,
and having attained the state of perfect cessation, they shall proceed to the abode of the Victors.
Thus, the worship of this Great Goddess, when performed with the recitation of the *hūṃ* syllable,
is established as a means for attaining the state of a Perfectly Awakened One, yielding exceedingly great merit.
Thus has the truth been declared by all the lords of sages;
having understood this, take refuge in and worship this Great Goddess.
Furthermore, the merit arising from the worship of this Dharmadhātu is established as even greater than that; it is the means for accomplishing the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Even for this Mañjudeva, the merit arising from worship has been declared to be exceedingly great; it is the proven means for attaining the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thinking thus, if you have the desire for the state of the Sugata,
all of you, having composed yourselves, should worship here in this temple of the Jina.
Having taken refuge in the Great Goddess Khagānanāsyā,
and having meditated upon her, recollected her, and even uttered her name, we have attained freedom from existence.

Those who, remaining in their refuge, having meditated upon and recollected them with concentrated minds, always worship them by even uttering their names throughout all existences; Svayambhū Purāṇa 3.158.
Those fortunate ones never go to an evil rebirth;
always born into a good rebirth, they become the locus of glory and virtue.
May the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who practice for the sake of awakening and the true Dharma,
and who are dedicated to the welfare of all sentient beings, become the sons of the Sugata.
Thus, for them, great happiness— endowed with auspicious glory and virtuous qualities— always proceeds in a state of composure, free from any calamity.
No fear of divine portents exists for them on any side;
seeing them thus endowed, all the gods, led by Indra, protect them with joy.
No fear of fire-omens shall ever exist for them,
because upon seeing them, the fires will always remain propitious and protect them.
Nowhere do they have any fear of untimely death;
for even Yama, having beheld them, protects them with favor.
For them, there is no safety from the Rākṣasa on any side,
such that even the winds, as his constant followers, would protect them by fanning them.
Not even for a yakṣa is there ever any fear from them anywhere;
on the contrary, all the yakṣas, even the lords of yakṣas, will guard them upon seeing them.
They have no fear from any quarter, even from other beings;
were even Īśāna to behold them, he would protect them with great joy.
There is no fear whatsoever for them regarding the birth of a Gandharva;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, too, seeing them, will protect them once he has been propitiated.
They never have any fear even of the kumbhāṇḍas;
seeing Virūḍhaka and the others, they are protected by his grace.
They have no fear of even the *nāgas* at any time or place;
for Virūpākṣa, being thoroughly propitiated, protects them with complete success.
They never have any fear of even the yakṣas anywhere;
for Kuvera, having observed them, has become well-disposed toward them and protects them.
They never have fear even from the *kiṃnaras*;
the great beings (*mahāsattvas*) look upon trees with favor, as if they were their benefactors.
There is no fear even from the Guhyakas for those who possess the sublime Dharma;
Vajrapāṇi, perceiving their welfare, will always be well-disposed toward them.
Likewise, they have no fear even of the Vidyādharas,
because Sarvārthasiddha himself always regards them with favor.
For them, there is never any fear of planetary portents or calamities;
for all the lords of the planets, having observed them, shall always protect them.
Likewise, no fear of portents such as the appearance of clusters of stars exists for them;
for all those stars, upon seeing them, flee everywhere until the end of existence.
The Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Rudras always behold them and approach them;
yet they never have any fear even of those beings at any time.
And likewise, there shall never be any danger from disturbances caused by the Mātṛkās;
for upon seeing all the Mātṛkās, they, being propitiated, will protect them.
Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and even the Bhairavas,
having beheld them at all times and being well-pleased, shall protect them.
Even the pretas, bhūtas, piśācas, vetāḍas, and hosts of ḍākinīs,
having beheld them at all times, shall protect them with favor.
Even from those [obstacles], there is never any fear for them;
for all of them shall be accompanied by their helpers in the accomplishment of the Dharma of perfect enlightenment.
They shall never have fear from lions and other beasts, nor from birds on all sides, nor from serpents, worms, or insects.
They have no fear whatsoever from wicked adversaries, nor from thieves, nor from enemies in any direction.
When those who are stained by merit behold her, they become serene;
all of them, bound by friendliness, compassion, and affection, shall become seekers of their own welfare.
In this way, all sentient beings, having seen them, become filled with serene faith;
with faces softened by affection and clear with joy, they shall behold them through the cultivation of loving-kindness.
And even kings, upon seeing them, being imbued with friendliness and affection,
with very serene intentions and joyful, shall always honor them with delight.
The ministers, too, should always speak with loving-kindness and affection toward them,
honoring them according to their desire as they practice the vows and means for accomplishing the True Dharma.
And all those brahmins, seeing their accomplishment of the true Dharma, rejoiced in their hearts and always bestowed auspicious blessings upon them.
Likewise, all the sages, seeing her, were filled with serene joy;
beholding her with compassionate eyes, they would gladden her with auspicious blessings.
And thus there are yogins, perfected ones, ascetics, celibates,
heretics, forest-dwellers, those who observe vows, and lay practitioners.
The monks, as well as the nuns and laywomen of Caira,
having beheld her with joyful vision, would gladden her with auspicious blessings.
And thus all the śrāvakas, as well as the pratyekabuddhas and all the bodhisattvas, having seen them, were filled with serene faith.
Beholding [beings] with compassion, those whose nature is imbued with loving-kindness and affection should always protect them on the paths to awakening and establish them in existence.
Thus, all the perfectly awakened ones, having seen her and being thoroughly gladdened,
shall always protect her with compassion and cause her to move for the welfare of the world.
Thus, for them, there is great merit that accomplishes the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha,
bestowing the attainment of auspicious glory, the perfection of virtues, prosperity, and spiritual success.
Thus, you too, having understood this, should always take refuge [in them],
and having honored them according to your ability, worship these Three Jewels.
Always with joy, having remembered, meditated upon, and even uttered the names of these very Three Jewels, remain established in refuge and venerate them.
Those who are anointed with this merit, whose three spheres are completely purified,
and who are endowed with the qualities of auspicious glory, shall become possessed of virtuous intentions.
May they never go to an evil rebirth, but always arise in a good rebirth;
may they become Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who practice the conduct of the Bhadrakalpa.
Then, intent on accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings, those steadfast ones,
having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order, [attained it].
Then, having conquered the hosts of Māra, being free from afflictions and having mastered their senses,
those Arhats attained the threefold enlightenment and went to the abode of the Victors.
All this has been proclaimed by me and by all the lords of sages;
having heard it and expressed your approval, always practice that which is auspicious.
Having heard this which was thus commanded by the Lord of Sages,
all those seated in the assembly rejoiced accordingly, awakened by the attainment of bliss.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Drying Up of the Great Lake and the Establishment of the Lotus Mountain in the Dharmadhātu," from the *Śrī Svayambhūtpatti-samuddeśa*.
The Fourth Chapter: The Narrative of the Origin of the Śrī Svayambhū Caitya, Titled "The Establishment of the Realm of the Tīrtharāja Free from Passion.
Now, that great being Maitreya, the son of the Sugata—
Bowing to the Blessed One with her hands joined in the añjali mudrā, she spoke thus: Svayambhū Purāṇa 4.1.
When did the Blessed One establish the succession of villages, towns, cities, and so forth, as well as the great provinces? He should deign to instruct us on that.
When Maitreya had thus made his request, the Blessed One, having heard it and gazed upon that one of great supernormal knowledge, gave this instruction: Svayambhū Purāṇa 4.3.
"Excellent! Listen attentively, O Great Being Maitreya;
I shall fully explain that time when my dwelling was here."
When the lifespan of humans was forty thousand years,
there appeared Dharmarāja Krakucchanda, the Lord of the World and Sovereign of Sages.
The master of all sciences, the Teacher, the guide of the three realms,
the omniscient Tathāgata, the Victor, has become possessed of the superknowledges.
The Fully Awakened One, for the sake of the welfare of the world, together with his assembly of disciples,
[resided] in a delightful great park outside the great city of Kṣemavatī.
In the monastery, the abode of the Sugata, he dwelt, illuminating it and teaching the True Dharma, which is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end.
At that time, I was the wise Bodhisattva named Jyotipāla;
having propitiated the Teacher Krakucchanda, I served him constantly.
Then that Blessed One, the Teacher Krakucchanda,
desiring to fully teach the True Dharma for the welfare of the world, set out among the provinces.
Then that Blessed One, the Teacher, accompanied by the entire community of monks,
conducted himself everywhere with auspiciousness, conversing as he moved along.
Thus wandering about, the Teacher taught the Dharma everywhere;
having gradually completed his journey here, he beheld all directions.
Having beheld this realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the blazing abode of the Jinas,
he joyfully took refuge in it together with the Saṅgha according to the prescribed rite.
Then that monk set out for this very place, the mountain named Śaṅkha,
and he resided upon a great, pure rock there.
There, he saw the Lord of the World, Krakucchanda, the Sovereign of Sages,
seated upon his throne in the midst of the assembly, honored by the community of monks.
Having beheld [him], the great beings, the sons of the Victors,
gathered together, filled with joy, to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Also the nun Śuśīlā and others, the Cailakas and the lay devotees (upāsakas),
the Cailakas who observe vows, and all the female lay devotees (upāsikās) as well.
The Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who long for the qualities of the True Dharma,
have all gathered here to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Having worshipped the Blessed One and performed circumambulations,
they bowed with palms joined in reverence there, and gazing upon him, they took their places nearby.
Likewise, Brahmā and the other great sages, ascetics, renunciants,
yogins, munis, and celibate students [also came].
In this way, Śakra and the other gods, all the lords of the world,
the planets, the hosts of stars, as well as the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Vidyādharas [are likewise].
Gandharvas, kinnaras, yakṣas, guhyakas, and even rākṣasas;
dānavas, garuḍas, and nāgas—likewise others have assembled here.
Having worshipped the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha, they were filled with joy;
having bowed down, they stood there with concentrated minds to drink the nectar of the Dharma.
And thus, O wise ones, there were Brahmins, as well as Kṣatriya kings, Vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, soldiers, servants, and other people as well. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 4.24)
Among householders, the wealthy, the virtuous, and the great men are preeminent;
so too are artisans, merchants, caravan leaders, and the citizens.
The subjects, the rural folk, the weary travelers, the pilgrims,
and likewise other people who had gathered from all directions.
Having beheld the Blessed One, they approached him, bowed down,
honored him in due order, and also performed circumambulations.
Having performed an eight-limbed prostration with palms joyfully joined,
he stood all around in that assembly to drink the nectar of its sublime Dharma.
Turning around, placing him at their head, and taking refuge in him with concentrated minds,
they sat down after honoring that Lord of Sages and gazing up at him.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled and perceiving the Noble Truths, taught the True Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, they were all awakened;
being filled with serene faith, they all desired to undertake the vow of the conduct of enlightenment.
Then, having fully understood his intention and perceiving that he was a Bodhisattva whose very nature was the essence of the path, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, spoke thus.
Noble son, even those who, out of joy and faith in the bull of the Sugatas,
desire to go forth into homelessness, are devoted to that very going forth.

In this regard, those who, through the secondary influence [of this teaching], practice the vow of awakening within the Buddhist dispensation, shall indeed achieve the fulfillment of all goals and purposes. (SvayambhuP 4.34)
They were all liberated from their transgressions, purified in the three spheres,
free from afflictions, stainless in nature, Bodhisattvas who had conquered their senses.
Having conquered the wicked hosts of Māra and slain those who violate the holy life,
they shall attain the threefold ocean of wisdom and reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thinking thus, those who desire perfect peace in this saṃsāra should go forth into homelessness there and, with faith, observe the Buddhist vow.
Having heard this instruction given by the Lord of Sages,
those great beings seated in the assembly were awakened and desired to go forth into the religious life.
Then he gave four hundred Brahmins, beginning with Guṇadhvaja,
as well as three hundred Kṣatriyas who were bestowers of fearlessness.
Likewise, many great beings— vaiśyas, śūdras, and virtuous people—
all of them being well-pleased, desired to go forth into the religious life.
Then they all rose up and, having approached with palms joined in reverence, bowed to the Blessed One and made this request with great devotion: Svayambhūpurāṇa 4.41.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, having received your command,
we desire to go forth into the Buddhist teaching and practice the vow.
O Blessed One, beholding us all with a compassionate eye, you ought to look upon us with favor and enjoin us to the True Dharma.
When they had all thus entreated him, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looking upon them all with a benevolent mind, addressed them collectively and commanded as follows.
If you desire to go forth into homelessness here in this Dharma of the Sugata, then, having gone forth, practice the vow of the Sugata everywhere.
Having thus instructed him, the Fully Awakened One, touching his head with his hand,
attentively established them all in the Dharma of the Sugata.
Then, having had their hair shorn and donning red robes,
they all took up alms-bowls made of *khikhirī* wood and became monks.
Then that Blessed One, having correctly taught those ascetics the true dharmas conducive to perfect enlightenment, bestowed upon them the vow of awakening.
Then those pure-souled ones, free from afflictions and with stainless faculties,
were devoid of desire for honor or gain, liberated from attachment, and untainted.
Their conduct toward themselves and others is equal; they are free from longing for the courses of saṃsāra;
they are unattached to the practices of Māra; and they regard a clod of earth and gold as the same.
The afflictions were stainless in nature, the three spheres were completely pure,
and the Arhats became auspicious practitioners of holy conduct.
Then all those Buddhist ascetics, practitioners of the path to enlightenment,
having acted for the benefit of all sentient beings, continued to dwell constantly in what is wholesome.
Then those of purified self, possessing the five superknowledges and great supernatural powers,
became venerable and worthy of worship for the worlds including the gods, serving as their gurus.
And at that time, from the thumb of Vajrasattva on the summit of that Śaṅkha mountain, pure water issued forth.
Thus, O Adbhuti, she became a great river with holy bathing places and a flowing current,
which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life upon all people.
Furthermore,
the purity of the words of the teaching of the True Dharma by that Lord Krakucchanda became manifest.
Therefore, she is renowned as the Vāgmatī, the foremost of all sacred fords;
she is the sustainer of auspicious glory and virtues, and the purifier of all sins.
Those who, having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, perform the libations for the ancestors and the gods, give gifts and the like, and also observe their vows; ||| SvayambhuP_4.58 |||
Those whose souls are stainless through the Sangha, endowed with the excellent qualities of auspicious glory,
having experienced happiness according to their desire, proceed to the abode of the Jinas.
Thinking thus, they should always bathe there, perform the libations for their ancestors and others,
practice charity and self-restraint, and move about for the welfare of the world.
By the mere sight of her at Pītāmbara, and even by touching her, all sins whatsoever are destroyed. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 4.61)
Even by merely rinsing one's mouth there, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā;
and by the mere sight of the stone, the six sense faculties become purified within the inner sanctum.
Thus, the merit arising from worshipping the Vāgmatī is far greater;
it is declared by the Jinas to be the best of all sacred sites (tīrtha), yet that [merit] does not belong to the Vāgmatī alone.
Thinking thus, those who always desire auspiciousness in this saṃsāra should at all times worship Vāgmatī, the glorious support of happiness. (SvayambhuP 4.64)
Furthermore, another river was born from his very hand;
she too was purified by the word of Krakucchanda.
There, regarding the facial hair, head hair, and nails of those who had gone forth into homelessness,
they divided them into two portions and cast one portion into that [water].
At that time, that great river became famous as Keśāvatī;
however, one portion of it remained established right there upon the rocky surface.
As many as there were hairs on his beard and head, so many caityas appeared upon the stone surface; indeed, they remain even today.
That river, too, became renowned as the great pilgrimage site Vāgmatī,
indeed through the power of the great merit of those renunciants.
Then, the great fame and sound of the merit of those renunciants, the monks who lived the holy life, spread everywhere.
Immediately after that, eight dispassionate ones, without support,
having the nature of light and formless, appeared for the welfare of the world.
One [liṅga] on the side of Śaṅkhagiri, near the hermitage of Maṇicūḍa, is renowned as Maṇiliṅga; it remains well-established even today.
The second is at Gokarṇa on the shore, having the form of a flame;
the third is on Mount Cāru, and the fourth is at Kumbhatīrtha.
The fifth is Phaṇiśaila, the sixth is Gartakasthala,
the seventh is at Gandhavatī, and the eighth is at Vikramasthala.
These eight great gods, free from passion and stainless,
whose nature is light and who are formless, have appeared for the welfare of the world.
Here, through the power of those who are free from passion, this delightful earth has arisen on all sides throughout the entire ground described as the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Then there was King Āyobhū, born of the lineage of Mahāsvo and Mahāsaṃmata; a Bodhisattva, whose nature was auspicious through compassion and pity.
There, that king, the lord of kings, came together with Krakucchanda the Protector to behold the Self-Existent One who has the face of a bird.
Having beheld the self-arisen abode of the Jina from afar,
he prostrated himself, approached, and performed three circumambulations.
Then, with great enthusiasm, one should worship this [image] consisting of the five Jinas.
Having prostrated with the eight limbs and taken refuge, he offered his devotion;
then likewise did the lord of kings to Mañjudeva and the true guru.
Having worshipped her according to the prescribed rites, that king of kings, filled with great joy, then offered his devotion to the Lordess of Victors, Khagānanā.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites, he honored them all with great enthusiasm and joy;
then he himself approached the eight Vītarāgas, who were all self-arisen (Svayambhūs).
Having seen this, King Samudita,
being virtuous and possessed of a great intention for merit, devoted himself with great enthusiasm to these meritorious acts through their power.
The sovereign lord of all dharmas, the ruler of all worlds,
shone forth as the king of all vidyās, Bhadraśrī, the refuge of excellent virtues.
Because of that, Dharmākara became renowned by name in Virājita;
thereafter, that great king desired to establish himself there.
Having bowed thus to Krakucchanda, the Lord of Sages, he made this request:
"O Blessed One, may you, the Teacher, understand my desire."
"Having obtained his permission, he ought to show me this favor.
When he had thus entreated him, the Blessed One, that lord of sages, [responded].
Beholding that king Dharmākara, he spoke thus:
"Excellent, O King, Great Being, that you desire this! (Svayambhūpurāṇa 4.89)
Abiding here in suchness, protecting and awakening the subjects,
he established all the worlds in that same state while fully enlightening them.
Having established them on the path to enlightenment, always practice what is auspicious;
protect all the worlds through the Dharma, practicing it yourself.
Dwell happily as you desire in your palace, for the welfare of the world;
always acting for the benefit of the world, remain established in the principles of Dharma.
Accomplishing the equipment for enlightenment, dwell always relying upon this body;
remaining forever in the refuge of this self-arisen Dharmadhātu.
Having performed worship with faith, conduct yourself for the welfare of the world,
having taken refuge in this goddess Khagānanā.
Having performed worship at all times, practice the vow of awakening,
relying upon this very Mañjudeva, the true guru.
Upholding the instruction of the Buddha, you should always conduct yourself within the true Dharma,
as well as among these eight who are free from passion.
Having performed worship with faith,
accomplish the supreme Dharma by resorting to the sacred sites (tīrthas) headed by the Vāgmatī.
Having performed ablutions, giving, and other rites, and having gratified the ancestors and the gods,
he attained purification of the three bodies and maintained the mind set on perfect enlightenment.
"Having brought benefit to all sentient beings, dwell at ease;
O Indra among kings, thus awaken all the worlds as well."
Having always established all of these within the sanctuary,
one should cause them to be attended to with respect, through worship, devotion, and great enthusiasm.
Establishing them on the path to enlightenment, always practice what is wholesome;
by doing so, O Great King, you will have made perfect enlightenment your refuge.
Having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, proceed for the welfare of the world;
with your self anointed by this merit, you will become a son of the Victors.
The Bodhisattva Mahābhijñā Bhadraśrī, who is the refuge of excellent qualities,
has never at any time wandered into an evil rebirth.
He is born with a constant and true course of conduct, possessed of prosperity and spiritual perfection,
wise, illustrious, the sovereign of all virtues, the lord of all worlds, and the author of all deeds.
Having gradually fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment,
one who is concentrated always experiences the bliss of great joy through the zeal of honoring the Three Jewels.
Consuming [alms] with pure conduct, abiding in the four sublime states (brahmavihāras),
free from afflictions and having conquered all Māras, he attained the state of an Arhat.
Having attained the threefold awakening, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
and may all worlds likewise become completely pure in the three spheres.
Bodhisattvas, the great beings, always arise in the higher realms;
having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, they move about for the welfare of the world.
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra, they dwell in the four sublime abodes;
free from afflictions, pure in nature, they have no longing for the course of saṃsāra.
The Arhats, having attained the threefold awakening, shall achieve Buddhahood;
and this applies even now to these eight who are free from passion.
O King, listen as I shall explain the specific excellence of the fruit of worship:
he who, being constantly composed, bathes daily in the waters of Vāgmatī; SvayambhuP_4.111.
One should always worship these eight great lords who are free from passion;
by that merit, one becomes a purified soul, endowed with prosperity, wealth, and happiness.
Having enjoyed constant happiness in saṃsāra, he shall go to the abode of Śiva—
he who bathes the self-arisen ones, free from passion, with ghee.
He who bathes the self-existent deities, who are free from passion, with curd, shall go to the abode of Śiva, as well as to Madhurā, the temple of Brahmā.
He shall indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu, which is the refuge of prosperity, abundance, and happiness;
even by bathing with sugarcane juice and so forth, he shall attain the station of a Vidyādhara.
With scented water, O Gāndharva, one attains the state of the Moon; with milk, one becomes pure in soul;
and with cold water, one becomes free from sin and possesses stainless senses.
And whoever should perform their worship with various fragrant flowers,
that lord of men, having enjoyed every pleasure and desire, rejoices.
One who unweariedly offers the most excellent bilva leaves and the rohiṇa-arcana attains Śiva everywhere and the merit of a thousand sacrifices.
He who offers the food offering shall become long-lived, O King Bali;
and he who offers a garland of lamps shall be radiant and possess excellent vision.
For one who burns guggulu resin, all sins are destroyed;
and he who gives an offering of sesame seeds shall not go to an evil rebirth.
He who gives gold shall always go to the assembly [of the gods],
and he who gives a sesame-cow shall go to the abode of Śiva.
He who gives away a tawny cow with silver hooves, golden horns, and adorned with a string of tinkling bells,
along with her calf, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
He who gives a jeweled cloak shall possess many jewels;
by the gift of clothing one becomes possessed of clothing, and by the gift of land one becomes possessed of land.
He who has attained divine hearing should promote great festivals involving instrumental music, song, dance, and so forth; he shall become an attendant at the side of Śiva.
He who offers blue lotuses, sun-flowers, and red lotuses shall obtain prosperity;
he who worships with bilva leaves shall become powerful and successful.
Having warded off the *dhattūraka* with which [the forest] was filled, which hero honored all the trees as well as the two women with fragrant flowers? (Svayambhūpurāṇa 4.126)
In the Saugandhita hermitage, he shall become illustrious, fortunate, and wise;
divine and exceedingly beautiful, beloved, endowed with auspicious glory, and possessed of excellent virtues.
Whoever worships the Śivas with flowers, leaves, fruits, roots, or hymns,
shall reach the abode of the gods and, having enjoyed divine bliss, proceed [to higher realms].
And whoever, having performed a circumambulation, should always worship with devotion,
he shall become beautiful in form at the end and proceed to the abode of Śiva.
And whoever, with a serene soul, should worship these Great Lords with hymns of praise,
he, having gone to the abode of the Pitṛs, shall obtain the bliss of great joy.
And whoever, having recited and chanted [the name] with a concentrated mind,
shall become glorious and possess great supernormal knowledge, and in the end go to the abode of Śiva.
He who, having performed prostration with the eight limbs, worships those Great Lords,
shall go only to a state of union [with them] and never to an evil rebirth.
Whoever, having remembered, meditated upon, and recited [the mantra], always worships even the Name,
shall enjoy divine nectar and rejoice in heaven according to his pleasure.
And whoever, having seen [it], bows down with a joyful heart and palms joined in reverence,
he too, having partaken of divine nectar, shall rejoice in heaven together with the gods.
Thus, having understood the certain superior fruit resulting from the worship of these eight who are free from passion, worship them according to your desire.
Therefore, having purified this earthly realm and established a city as your refuge,
dwell here forever, supporting all the worlds and protecting them at all times.
Then, from all directions, all the people of the world, filled with joy, will come here,
establish their residence, and dwell forever in delight.
Then, the people of the countryside, as well as the villages and cities,
would also set out from all sides toward the place of cremation.
Likewise, the gods and the lords of the asuras, as well as all the rulers of the worlds,
having come here and beheld the self-arisen Dharmadhātu, [were filled with wonder].
Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Rākṣasas as well;
Kumbhāṇḍas, Garuḍas, Nāgas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas too.
The Sādhyas, the Mātṛkās, and the hosts of Bhairavas as well;
the Ṛṣis, the Yogins, the ascetics, and even the Tīrthikas.
The Śrāvakas, the Bhikṣus, the Arhats, and also the Upāsakas such as the Cailakas;
the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and likewise the Śaivas, Kaulas, and Vaiṣṇavas.
Having come here and beheld the self-arisen Dharmadhātu, as well as the goddess Khagānanā and his venerable teacher Mañjuśrīdeva; SvayambhuP_4.143.
Having taken refuge in these beings who are free from passion and in the power of the sacred fords,
they should always worship them with joy.
Then, through the power of all their merit, there will certainly be abundance, auspiciousness, and enthusiasm for all these Daityas here,
and it shall be free from calamities.
Having heard these instructions from Krakucchanda, the lord of sages, Dharmākara agreed, saying, "So be it," and understood accordingly.
Then that king, rising with palms joined in reverence, bowed to the Lord of Sages, Krakucchanda, together with his assembly, and addressed him thus:
O Blessed One, having received your command, I shall indeed always dwell here,
having established a city for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
Therefore, may you, out of compassion, look upon this Himālaya and,
having taught the Dharma here always together with your community, dwell for the welfare of the world.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages, looking toward the Great Being Dharmākara, spoke as follows: Svayambhū Purāṇa 4.150.
I shall not remain here forever;
I shall wander over the entire earth, for I have become one who points the way to the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having thus instructed Krakucchanda, that leader of sages,
the latter then set out for another region and traveled along, conversing with others.
Then Dharmākara, having constructed a city there in that manner and established the constituent elements of sovereignty, ruled the kingdom and presided over it.
Then all of them, having arrived here from all sides and taken refuge in the temples,
established their residence and lived there in joy.
Then others also arrived there from all directions and from everywhere.
They lived joyfully in many villages throughout the city and the countryside.
Likewise, all the gods, the asuras and others, and even the lords of the worlds,
having arrived here together with their respective retinues, dwell here with joy.
Likewise, there were great seers, ascetics, celibate students,
yogis, mendicants, arhats, observers of vows, and lay devotees as well.
The Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, and even the Śrāvakas,
having performed their labors, took up residence in whatever places they desired.
Likewise, other non-Buddhist practitioners— the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, and even the Kaulikas—
established hermitages and took up residence in places according to their own desires.
The Pratyekabuddhas and Sugatas also gathered from all sides,
taking up residence with joy in that secluded and delightful hermitage.
Even the lords of sages, having arrived here and dwelt together with their retinues,
attained supreme enlightenment and, after teaching the true Dharma, departed in haste.
Thus, this most meritorious land, called Himālayāhava,
is as delightful as Sukhāvatī and is the refuge of Bodhisattvas.
Moreover, many sacred fords (tīrthas) exist here that remove all sins;
they have arisen as bestowers of the perfection of all goals and prosperity.
Therefore, bathe in these sacred fords and practice virtuous vows,
O men who desire here to destroy evil and attain auspiciousness.
Those who, having always bathed with a concentrated mind in all these sacred fords, perform recitations, sacrifices, and other rites, and observe their vows; SvayambhuP_4.165.
Having worshipped both the ancestors and the gods with faith and reverence,
and having given gifts and composed themselves, they also meditate upon and worship the Lord.
They all shall be free from blemish, with the three spheres completely purified;
they shall be glorious, possessed of accomplishment, and the abode of excellent qualities.
Then, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, those sons of the Sugata would become Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who accomplish the Dharma.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for awakening in due order and having rendered service to the Three Jewels, they should move about for the welfare of the world.
Then those pure-souled ones, free from afflictions and having conquered their senses,
shall become Arhats and attain the threefold enlightenment and the state of the Sugata.
Thinking thus, those who desire awakening should always perform acts such as giving after bathing in all these sacred fords throughout their existence.
Having heard this command thus imparted by the Lord of Sages,
all the people gathered in the assembly, being enlightened, rejoiced.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Propagation of the Realm of the Tīrtha of the Passionless One," from the *Śrī Svayaṃbhū-caitya-samutpatti-kathā*.

The Fifth Chapter: Titled "A Description of the Great Majesty of the Merit Arising from the Many Tīrthas Born of the Manifestation of the Self-Existent One" (*Svayambhūtpatti-anekatīrthasaṃjāta-puṇyamahātmya-varṇana*).
Now, that Great Being Maitreya, with palms joined in reverence and with joy...
Having bowed to that Blessed One, one should pray thus with devotion: (Svayambhūpurāṇa 5.1)
O Blessed One, please now explain the specific excellence of the fruit of merit arising from acts such as giving after bathing at those sacred fords.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, looking toward the Great Being Maitreya, gave this instruction: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 5.3.
"Excellent! Listen, O Mahāsattva, to the arising of the fruit of serving sacred fords (tīrthas).
I shall explain that specific merit for the sake of awakening all."
For instance, twelve primary pilgrimage sites (tīrtha) are mentioned here,
which are indeed the most meritorious among all the sacred sites on earth.
At the confluence of the Vāgmatī, which bestows unfailing fruit,
there is the famous sacred site known as Śodhana, because it purifies the ten types of sin.
There, the lord of the nāgas named Takṣaka is red and exceedingly beautiful,
adorned with a majestic hood blazing with great jewels.
By whatever faith people may perform a bath according to the prescribed rite at that holy ford with joy for twenty-one days; Svayambhūpurāṇa 5.8.
They should perform rites such as recitation and sacrifice for even seven days;
having fully worshipped the ancestors and the gods, they should render them completely satisfied and joyful.
They should respectfully give gifts to those who ask according to their desires;
and, possessing pure conduct, they should likewise practice their vows with concentrated minds.
Through this purification of merit, those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, shall become free from afflictions, with stainless faculties,
and abodes of glorious virtues.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
and having attained the threefold enlightenment, they shall reach the state of perfect buddhahood.
And thereafter, where the Vāgmatī joins with the Māradāyinī,
that is known as Śāntatīrtha, which purifies the defects of the afflictions.
There, the lord of the nāgas is white, renowned as Somaśikhi;
he is adorned with a circle of hoods possessing the splendor of shimmering jewel-gems.
There too, O Śānta, those men who are afflicted by the afflictions (kleśa) should always perform ablutions at the sacred ford (tīrtha) for twenty-one days.
They should perform recitations, sacrifices, and the like, and observe the poṣadha vows;
having fully honored the ancestors and the gods, they should remain satisfied and joyful.
They should joyfully give gifts to supplicants according to their desires;
possessing pure conduct and right behavior, they should meditate upon and worship the Lord.
Anointed with this merit, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, whose three spheres are completely purified, shall become abodes of glorious virtues.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
those three kinds of Arhats shall attain enlightenment and reach the state of the Sugata.
And then, at the confluence of the Maṇirohiṇī and the Vāgmatī,
there [is a stream] issuing upwards, resembling a pure crystal pillar.
The stream of Rudra is called Mṛta;
by that [confluence] at that meeting point, it is known as the Triveṇī confluence, and thus it is called the Śaṅkara Tīrtha.
There, Śaṅkhapāla, the lord of the nāgas, was exceedingly beautiful;
he shone with jewels and was adorned with glorious hoods.
In that Śaṅkara-tīrtha, those men who perform their ritual ablutions with joy according to the prescribed rule for twenty-one days; SvayambhuP_5.23.
They should perform rites such as recitation and sacrifice for seven days, worshiping the ancestors and the gods and offering libations according to the prescribed rule. (Svayambhu Purāṇa 5.24)
Those whose minds are set on awakening should give gifts with faith to those who ask;
having meditated, they should worship the Lord and practice the six-fold path.
Through this merit, may those of purified self, free from afflictions, and with stainless faculties,
obtain great prosperity, peace, virtuous qualities, and tranquility as well.
By that [merit], they shall never go to an evil rebirth; having come together, may these Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, always be practitioners of the auspicious conduct.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
those Arhats shall attain the threefold enlightenment and reach the state of the Sugata.
And then, where the Vāgmatī river meets the Rājamārgī,
that is declared to be Rājatīrtha, the source of sovereignty, health, and happiness.
There dwells the lord of the nāgas, white in color, renowned for his beautiful form and exceedingly handsome;
his body is adorned with the glorious radiance of the great brilliance of precious jewels.
There, those who are devoted to Maṇavāyu should perform bathing, giving, recitation, and meditation for twenty-one days, and they should also bestow the vow of restraint.
Purified by this merit, they shall be faultless and possess stainless faculties;
they shall attain sovereignty, power, constant health, auspiciousness, and happiness.
They too shall not go to an evil rebirth, but shall always be born in a good state;
these Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, shall become the locus of glorious virtues.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
those Arhats attained the threefold enlightenment and went to the abode of the Victors.
Likewise, at the confluence of the Vimalāvatī and Keśāvatī rivers here,
he fulfilled the wish expressed by her, bestowing upon her the ornament of her own desire.
There dwells the formidable lord of nāgas, known as Kulika, who is exceedingly magnificent;
his body is adorned with a glorious halo, brilliantly illuminated by the jewels upon his hoods.
There, at the Mano-ratha Tīrtha,
those men who perform bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites according to the prescribed rule for twenty-one days, [attain the fruit].
Those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who always arise in happy destinies and are the locus of auspicious glory and excellent virtues, shall never go to an evil destiny.
Adorned with ornaments according to their own desire— such as fine silks, garments, and jewels—
the Bodhisattvas should practice for the sake of establishing the welfare of all sentient beings.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
they shall attain the threefold enlightenment and reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
