Thus, this stage of great accomplishment, beautifully adorned with glory,
crowded with great beings, and the most excellent of all stages, shone forth.
Then, after some time, there was a king here named Śrī Guṇakāmadeva, a monarch who was a self-disciplined ascetic and a teacher who became a lord of the world.
Then that king, being mature, young, and exceedingly eager for desire,
enjoyed the essence of passion as he pleased and acted according to his own will.
Then that kṣatriya, likewise deluded by the pursuit of sensual pleasures and infatuated with the qualities of women, showed no regard for ethical conduct or dharma.
Having seen the beautiful Sundarī, though she was unapproachable, he was infatuated; having forcibly drawn her toward him, he enjoyed her at his pleasure with delight.
In this way, that king of men, excessively lustful for the objects of desire,
having entrusted all the constituents of sovereignty to his ministers, would take his pleasure according to his own will.
Then all those ministers, having established that king under the control of a woman, enjoyed themselves as they pleased and moved about according to their desire.
Likewise, all the servants and people, their intentions corrupted,
rejected the true teachings and lived devoted to sensual pleasures.
And likewise, all those brahmins practiced the ten unwholesome deeds;
having abandoned the boundaries of their own family dharma, they acted according to their own whims.
And likewise, the Vaiśyas, being greedy for the accumulation of wealth through unrighteous means,
abandoned the traditional livelihood of their own caste and lived as they pleased, consuming whatever they desired.
Likewise, all the great masses of people, acquiring wealth through unjust means and abandoning the dharma of their own lineage, lived happily merely by consuming it.
Likewise, all the merchants, striving to achieve their goals through falsehoods and rejecting the true Dharma, lived while intoxicated by the pride of their afflictions.
Likewise, all the artisans, greedy for their morsels of food,
ignorant of the proper rules and blinded by negligence, performed their work according to their own whims.
Likewise, even the womenfolk, afflicted by passion and driven by their family attachments,
abandoned the dharma of their own lineage and acted according to their own desires.
In this way, all the people as well, being addicted to the ten unwholesome actions,
abandoned the conduct of their own families and acted according to their own whims.
And even those wicked heretics, upon seeing this abode of the Jina,
reviled and censured it, and went about as they pleased.
At that time, many wicked thieves, rogues, and bold scoundrels,
having insulted virtuous people, roamed about like rutting elephants.
Even the virtuous and the noble, though they followed base occupations and had lost their enthusiasm for the true Dharma, lived like low-born men, eating whatever they could find.
Then, due to the proliferation of evil in this manner, Kali moved everywhere;
the True Dharma became weak and perished like something base.
Then, as the Kali age prevails here,
all the lords of the world, having seen it, become enraged and turn their faces away.
Then, turning away from him even though they were the lords of all the worlds, they cried out, "Shame on the king! and did not wish to look at him even.
Then, during that festival of the World-Protectors’ joyful vision,
calamities approached and began to prevail.
Then even the cruel gods who were wicked partisans of Māra,
beholding all those forms there, brought about a great portent.
The Fire-god also, having observed that, became enraged with a wicked intent;
with flames enveloped in smoke, he burned [the city] and brought about a great portent here.
The King of Dharma also became enraged;
merciless, he unleashed a great pestilence to strike down all living beings, even those free from disease.
The lord of the Rākṣasas from the southwest, exceedingly cruel and provoked to anger,
entered everywhere here and constantly brought about great portents.
Varuṇa, the king of the nāgas, was also provoked to anger with a cruel look.
Having seen clouds carrying water, one should ward off all rain.
The Maruts, having likewise observed this, stood there enraged and merciless;
performing what was impossible to achieve, they brought about a great portent here.
Likewise, those wicked yakṣas, as well as the kinnaras and guhyakas,
entered house after house and caused the outbreak of diseases.
Likewise, there were *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, *vetālas*, *kaṭapūtanas*, *ḍākinīs*, *pramathas*, and *śākinīs*, together with their hosts.
The Rudras, along with the Gandharvas, Kumbhāṇḍas, and Garuḍas,
roaming everywhere there, brought about a great portent.
All the Mothers as well, along with their retinues,
being displeased and seeing that they were all extremely wicked, did not endeavor to look upon them.
All the planets and hosts of stars were adverse and displeased;
they did not even desire to grant their vision or instruction.
All the goddesses who are the mistresses of the families, though not yet propitiated,
remained there simply by beholding them, capable of providing protection.
In this way, the other gods as well were averse to providing protection everywhere;
they did not even desire to grant them a vision of themselves.
Not even one among them was able to protect them in any way;
thus, a great calamity broke out here on all sides.
Thus, a great upheaval broke out here on all sides;
all the afflictions, their essence destroyed, engaged in mutual conflict.
Thus, having observed all the worlds stained by the Kali age and having meditated for a very long time, that king reflected thus in his mind: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 8.52.
"Alas, what a terrible suffering born of sin now arises for me here!
Who of noble intent would provide this means for the pacification of that sin? (SvayambhuP 8.53)
"How will this great suffering be pacified here? Seeing [this] thus, why should I remain indifferent and take my pleasure now? (Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.54)
For what king is he who, disregarding the suffering of his subjects, delights in pleasure;
is he not censured as a ruler and master who is like a venomous serpent?
Where a king, disregarding the suffering of his subjects, does not investigate it himself, but instead enjoys pleasure and wanders about as he pleases; SvayambhuP_8.56.
There, all the people of the world, their minds agitated by afflictions,
will abandon truth, dharma, family, and conduct, and act with arrogance.
Consequently, those who are stained by evil deeds and who practice the ten unwholesome actions,
being shameless even regarding great sins, will roam about according to their own desires.
"A king shall certainly enjoy all this great fortune"—
this is the truth declared by the great seers who are experts in political ethics.
"O Bhava, I must indeed experience this ripening of my evil karma;
therefore, what shall I do here, since you do not consider any means [to prevent it]?"
Fie on my birth in this saṃsāra, in whose kingdom there is constant strife and where great calamities such as famine prevail day and night! (Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.61)
Blessed are those men who are free from afflictions, whose intentions are stainless,
who have abandoned wandering through existence, and who are monks practicing the holy life.
What is the use of my birth in this cycle of existence, even though it was in a noble family for men,
since I, like a beast, merely enjoy sensual pleasures and take delight in the household?
Thus, defiled by this evil and with a mind agitated by afflictions, I would wander through the hells and constantly experience manifold suffering. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.64)
At that time, who would come forward as my friend or ally to protect me?
At that time, Dharma alone would be the refuge that removes all suffering.
The Buddha’s Dharma is the most excellent among all dharmas; it removes all fears, accomplishes all goals, is proven effective, and is proclaimed for the welfare of the world.
Thus, having gone now, I shall respectfully entreat the Great Master Śāntaśrī, who resides on Mount Gośṛṅga.
For that very Great Teacher, having prescribed this ritual for the pacification of these portents, shall always do what is beneficial for me in this matter.
Having thus resolved, the king summoned his domestic priest, the ministers, the great men, and the citizens, and commanded them as follows. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.69)
"O noble sirs, since such a great portent has arisen right here,
I now wish to perform the rite of Dharma that brings about its pacification."
Then, having respectfully entreated the teacher Śāntiśrī, who possesses great supernormal knowledge,
I wish to take away from that place one who is his equal.
Thus, we all, with great reverence, shall carry the Vajra there to the summit of Gośṛṅga in order to entreat the Great Master Śāntaśrī.
Having heard this command from the lord of men, the domestic priest and all the others, being thus enlightened, replied,
"So be it," and rejoiced.
Then that king, the lord of men, together with his ministers, the people, and the citizens,
placing the family priest at the head, joyfully proceeded to Gośṛṅga.
Having seen that teacher there, the king was filled with joy;
approaching him with palms joined in reverence, he bowed and took refuge at his lotus-feet.
Likewise, all the worlds, having beheld him and become serene,
gathered together, bowed at his feet, and stood before him with joy.
Having observed all of them gathered together, that highly intelligent Śāntaśrī, looking toward the protector of the earth, gave this instruction: Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.77.
"O King, may it always be well with you, uninterrupted in every respect. For what purpose have you come here? You ought to tell me that."
When Śāntaśrī had spoken thus, the king, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to that great teacher and, gazing upon him, made this submission: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 8.79.
"O illustrious Lord, for that purpose I have come to you for refuge;
please deign to instruct me here regarding that which I pray for."
"Since a great calamity has arisen in my kingdom due to my own sin,
you ought to instruct me in the means for pacifying it."
When the king had thus made his request, the wise Śāntaśrī, a knower of mantras, looked upon that Great Being, O King, and commanded him as follows: Svayambhū Purāṇa 8.82.
O King, because of such evil, a great portent arises right here;
I shall tell you the means for pacifying that evil—listen to it.
Since you, O King, though a ruler here who ought to protect all dharmas,
do not govern your subjects in accordance with the dharma of political ethics.
Likewise, the ministers, having turned their backs on all principles of policy and dharma,
indulge only in sensual pleasures and behave according to their own whims.
Likewise, servants, common people, citizens, and even great men,
having abandoned the dharma of their own families, conduct themselves according to their own whims.
In this way, all people in the world, practicing the ten unwholesome actions,
reject the true teachings and proceed through negligence.
Therefore, O Bhava, you must indeed experience this ripening of evil;
for by whomsoever an action was performed, by him alone must its fruit be experienced.
Thinking thus, the king, as his own master, reflecting according to political wisdom and having diligently instructed the people, should always protect them.
If, in this matter, the king, having failed to investigate properly due to negligence, [acts otherwise].
Having himself enjoyed the very pleasures of desire, he wanders about according to his will.
Likewise, all the people as well, following the conduct of kings,
would merely enjoy the pleasures of desire and behave according to their own whims.
Then, due to that evil, a great calamity will certainly arise there;
once the great calamity has arisen, the worlds will be afflicted by the suffering of sin.
In that situation, the king who looks on with indifference and acts without compassion,
being unattached to the protection of the world, shall partake of all their sins.
For indeed, all sins committed by all people in the world shall fall before the king and present their fruits to him.
Thus has the truth been fully declared by all the lords of sages;
having bowed, the king himself should act while reflecting according to political ethics.
Having heard this instruction from the minister Śāntaśrī,
the king’s heart was tormented by the heat of anxiety out of fear.
Having beheld that Teacher, the glory of peace, he went for refuge;
bowing again at his lotus feet, he made this request with great reverence.
O Teacher, I shall always carry out your command upon my head;
therefore, you ought to instruct me in that which is appropriate for me according to the Dharma.
Having heard this prayer made by the king, that teacher of noble mind, beholding the monarch who was a being of great virtue, gave him this instruction: Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.99.
O King, listen with a concentrated mind; I shall declare the cause of auspiciousness.
If you have compassion for the world, then do as I have spoken.
Just as by bathing daily according to the rules in these sacred fords (tīrthas),
one becomes pure in conduct and practice, composed, and perfected in the three spheres (trimaṇḍala).
Having made an aspiration for perfect awakening, bearing the welfare of all sentient beings in mind,
and having paid homage to the Three Jewels, observe the Poṣadha vow.
Therefore, having propitiated this Lord of the World, the Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Victors,
according to the prescribed ritual, always attend upon him with devotion.
Likewise, having propitiated and worshipped all these five deities according to the prescribed rule, enjoy them always with devotion.
And you too, Mañjuśrī, having propitiated this caitya at all times and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, enjoy it with great festivals.
Likewise, having properly propitiated the eight who are free from passion according to the prescribed rites,
honor them with great enthusiasm and always serve them with devotion.
Likewise, having propitiated and worshipped with due reverence the goddess Māheśvarī, who has the face of a bird, enjoy her according to the prescribed rite.
Indeed, all these gods, who are the sovereign lords of all worlds,
have truly manifested themselves for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Therefore, having always performed worship according to the prescribed rite with faith toward all these gods, proceed for the welfare of the world.
And having likewise diligently awakened all the worlds,
one should always perform bathing, giving, and other such rites at all these sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having performed this great merit which bestows auspiciousness, happiness, and welfare upon the world,
observe the Poṣadha vow for the sake of the true bliss of the qualities of a Perfect Buddha.
And having always performed the worship of these deities, such as the Three Jewels,
with great enthusiasm, cause them to proceed upon the path to enlightenment.
Then, by the power of this merit, as one moves auspiciously everywhere,
all great portents shall then go to dissolution in every place.
Then Brahmā, Indra, and all the other lords of the worlds,
beholding him here with a favorable eye, shall always protect him with joy.
Then, when this world is protected by all those lords of the world,
there shall indeed always prevail abundance, prosperity, auspiciousness, and enthusiasm.
Then all people shall be free from disease and endowed with glorious virtues;
having desisted from evil paths, they shall always proceed toward what is auspicious.
O King, by always maintaining this through the power of great merit,
they shall eventually attain awakening and reach the state of a perfect Buddha.
Having understood that such great merit arises from honoring the Three Jewels,
first honor the Three Jewels with faith and mindfulness.
Then, having bathed in all the sacred fords (tīrtha) with your senses and mind purified,
go for refuge to the Three Jewels and observe the Poṣadha vow.
Then, having always propitiated all these deities, headed by the Dharmadhātu, according to the prescribed ritual, enjoy them while offering worship.
Having thus diligently awakened all the worlds and having caused them to bathe in all these sacred fords according to the prescribed rites, ||| SvayambhuP_8.121 ||| he [proceeded].

Having established [them] in refuge in the Three Jewels, bestow upon them the Poṣadha vow, which is the means for attaining the wisdom of perfect enlightenment and the support of auspicious, glorious, and virtuous qualities.
Having ensured the constant worship of these deities as well,
and having established them on the path to enlightenment, practice and protect yourself in virtue.
Having performed this and attained great merit, one who is the refuge of the glorious and virtuous qualities will certainly become a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva endowed with the great superknowledges.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for perfect enlightenment in due order,
and having attained the state of an Arhat, you shall reach the station of a Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having heard this instruction given by the Teacher Śāntaśrī, the king replied, "So be it," and desired to act accordingly.
Then that king, having summoned all his ministers, counselors, people, citizens, and the great multitude, commanded them thus: Svayambhū Purāṇa 8.127.
"O ministers, all people, counselors, citizens, and great men,
you ought to act exactly as instructed by the Teacher."
I too, having always maintained that auspicious cause and having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, am eager to practice the vow.
Having heard this command from the lord of men, those ministers,
the people, and all the citizens replied, "So be it."
Then that king, accompanied by all his domestic priests, ministers, counselors, officials, citizens, and eminent men, [set out].
Having bathed in all these sacred fords in due order according to the prescribed rites, he,
being pure in conduct and composed, undertook the Poṣadha vow.
Then those pure-souled ones, having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
joyfully propitiated and worshipped the Dharmadhātu.
Likewise, he should worship the deities of Wind in Vāyupura according to the prescribed rite,
the god Agni in Agnipura, and the lords of the hooded serpents in Nāgapura.
In Vasupura, [one should worship] Vasundharā, who bestows the excellence of the true Dharma;
and in Śāntapura, Maheśāna and Saṃvara together with their retinues, in due order.
Just as one who, having worshipped according to the rules and relying with faith,
always worships and honors a caitya in that same manner, O Mañjuśrī.
Likewise, having propitiated the eight Vītarāgas and the goddesses Śrī and Khagānanā according to the prescribed rites, he worshipped them constantly with due honor.
Likewise, all those people, following the conduct of the king,
bathed with devotion in all the sacred fords and became pure in character.
Having taken refuge in the Three Jewels and observed the vows of the *poṣadha*,
they honored all the gods who have the Dharmadhātu as their gateway and devoted themselves to them.
Then, by the power of this merit, he performed auspicious deeds everywhere;
consequently, all those great portents gradually subsided.
Then all those people, free from disease and with their faculties nourished,
attained great joy and happiness, and became devoted to the Dharma.
Having seen that direct fruit of dharma, the king, the monarch, exclaimed, "Oh, the greatness of the true Dharma! and he proceeded, filled with joy.
At that time, there was no good rain at all;
seeing this, the king’s mind became apprehensive of a famine.
Then that king, his heart overcome with compassion,
bowed once more to the Teacher Śāntaśrī and spoke with palms joined in reverence:
By the grace of the Ācārya, auspiciousness now prevails here;
may every great calamity be pacified on all sides at all times.
"Good rain has not yet commenced in any way;
therefore, he ought to prescribe the means for bringing about good rain."
Having heard this request made by the king, that teacher of noble mind, looking upon the monarch who was possessed of great being, spoke thus: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 8.147.
"Excellent! O King, listen now to the cause for constant abundance and the means for bringing about good rain; I shall instruct you on this at once."
Having drawn the mandala of the nāga kings according to the prescribed rite,
one should invoke all the lords of the nāgas there and worship them.
Therefore, O great hero, become here a perfected practitioner who has transcended existence;
accomplish all things exactly as they were taught by Māyā.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, that king, with joy, replied,
"So be it," and desired that it should be so.
Then Vajradhṛk, having drawn the beautiful mandala in Nāgapura according to the prescribed rite, consecrated it and worshipped it.
There, having propitiated all the lords of the *nāgas* in due order and having summoned them, that master proceeded to worship and anoint them.
There, all the lords of the nāgas, having assembled in due order and occupied their respective seats, remained there with serene minds.
The serpent-king Karkoṭaka alone did not come out of shame;
seeing this, the Great Master Śāntaśrī, possessed of great supernatural power, [acted].

Having gazed upon that king, who was a great hero, a being of great essence, possessed of great supernatural power, and endowed with great higher knowledge, he addressed him and commanded as follows: Svayambhū Purāṇa 8.156.
"O King, all the lords of the nāgas have now assembled here;
only Karkkoṭaka, the king of the nāgas, has not come."
"I am deformed; how could I go and sit upon the great assembly throne of the Naga King?"—having reflected thus, he did not come out of shame. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.158)
Therefore, O King, go quickly to that great lake there,
address Karkkoṭaka, and having entreated him, bring him here.
If that king of serpents does not come here even when entreated,
then seize him by force and bring him back by all means.
Having heard these instructions from the teacher, that wise king, beholding the teacher Śāntaśrī, addressed him in this manner: Svayambhū Purāṇa 8.161.
"O Teacher, how might I, having gone there to that deep great lake,
be able to seize the lord of the nāgas by force and bring him here?"
Having been thus informed by the king, that preceptor, a knower of mantras, looked upon the great hero, the monarch, and spoke as follows. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.163)
Mounting the bay horse and holding the flower purified by my mantra, go forth;
you shall be able to do so through the power of my mantra.
"This is the Durvākuṇḍa flower; first cast it there while remembering me.
Wherever you wander, follow that flower as it moves. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.165)
Having thus instructed on the difficult-to-overcome sacrificial pit purified by mantras,
and having offered a flower to the lord of men, he further taught as follows:
Having gone there, O King, to that city of the Nāgas, approach Karkoṭaka and, having consulted with him,
report these words of mine.
"O Karkkoṭaka, Lord of Nagas, whatever purpose you have for coming here, you yourself must know it; nevertheless, I shall speak."
At Gośṛṅga, the great master Śāntaśrī, a virtuous wielder of the vajra,
is always present to bring about the pacification of famine and the bringing forth of good rain.
There, in Nāgapura, having propitiated all the lords of the nāgas according to the prescribed ritual and having summoned them, he began to worship them.
All the lords of the nāgas, beginning with Varuṇa, have assembled there;
why have you alone not come? It behoves you to go there immediately.
Even if that king of serpents should not come despite being thus entreated,
he must be forcibly dragged away and brought here by you immediately.
Thus, having been respectfully instructed by Śāntaśrī, I have been sent here for that purpose; therefore, you ought to come together there.
Having thus instructed him and given that flower purified by mantra,
the Ācārya sent the heroic king there with haste.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Teacher, that Mahāmati took up Durvāmuṇḍa, said "So be it," and then set out.
Then that heroic king, the foremost among rulers,
mounted his bay-horsed chariot and, moving about, went to that lake.
Having reached the shore there and beholding that lake, the king,
having bowed and recollected his preceptor, cast Durvākuṇḍa into the water.
Once thrown into shallow water, it floated about and moved toward Nāgapura;
the king, mounting his horse, followed those flowers as they went.
Having thus gone to Nāgapura and searching about,
that king suddenly approached Karkoṭaka, the lord of the earth.
Having approached the lord of Karkoṭaka there,
that hero reported everything exactly as he had been instructed by his preceptor.
Having heard all that was thus reported, even that lord of the nāgas gave no reply whatsoever to the king.
Then that king, having thus informed the lord of the earth,
gazed upon him, addressed him, and entreated him with great devotion.
O Lord of Nagas, be gracious here; bear the command of the Teacher upon your head.
It was only at your invitation that I previously came; therefore, return there with me.
Although he was thus entreated, that king, the lord of serpents,
gave no reply whatsoever to the monarch.
Then that heroic king, having reported everything before him exactly as it was prescribed in the scriptures and other sources, spoke again in this manner:
O Lord of Nagas, it was no fault of mine that my words were not heard by you;
for I would surely have acted exactly as instructed by the scriptures.
Even when addressed thus by the lord of men, that very Karkoṭaka gave no answer at all to the king, the upholder of the earth.
Then that heroic king, bearing the Teacher’s command upon his head,
seized that serpent and proceeded like Garuḍa.
Then, having been brought from that horse by Guṇakāmadeva, he was led along that path;
thus it is called Vaśikācala.
Having thus seized and dragged that lord of the earth,
the hero suddenly led him to Nāgapura and presented him before the Teacher.
"O Teacher, at your command, the serpent-king Karkkoṭaka was seized and dragged away by me; having seen him, may you be gracious. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 8.191)
Having heard what was thus reported by the king, the teacher became composed;
looking upon that great hero, the monarch, he instructed him as follows: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 8.192.
"Excellent, O King, great hero! Since this serpent has been brought by you from the netherworld, lead him to his seat and establish him there in due order."
Having heard these instructions given by the Teacher, the king likewise addressed that Nāga king and seated him upon his own throne.
Seeing her seated upon her own throne, that teacher,
having duly invoked those lords of the nāgas, propitiated them and honored them.
Then that preceptor, the lord of the earth, who was the protector of Vraja,
having praised all the lords of the nāgas, made this request with great reverence.
O noble ones, all you great Naga kings have been propitiated, summoned, and duly honored by me in your presence.
May they always be gracious to me and grant my desire;
it is for the sake of the welfare of the entire world that I propitiate them, and not otherwise.
Because of the prevalence of evil here, a famine now prevails;
therefore, all people, afflicted by suffering, commit sinful acts.
For the sake of pacifying that famine and for the constant cause of abundance,
I shall always employ this means of bringing about good rain for the welfare of the world.
Therefore, all of you here are capable of bringing about constant, excellent rain for the protection of all sentient beings.
Having heard this request made by Śāntaśrī,
all the lords of the nāgas replied to him, "So be it."
Having heard that the nāga kings had promised "so be it," Śāntaśrī then earnestly entreated those nāga kings in this manner: Svayambhū Purāṇa 8.203.
May you, sirs, be gracious to me once more regarding that which I pray for;
they ought to grant even that desired boon for the welfare of all sentient beings.
When he, Śāntaśrī, had thus made his supplication,
all the lords of the nāgas, having heard him, promised him "So be it."
Having heard that promise made by all those lords of the nāgas, the Ācārya requested those serpent-kings with such earnestness: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 8.206.
Sirs, listen to the words that I request once more:
that which was promised by you must always be fulfilled accordingly.
When, due to the movement of malevolent planets, a poor rainfall should certainly occur,
then let that rite for the accomplishment of good rain be performed.
Just as it has been written upon your banner, I am prepared to establish and consecrate an auspicious maṇḍala according to the prescribed ritual.
If there should be drought even here, then one should likewise spread out the silk mandala,
worship it according to the ritual, invoke [the deities], and perform the offerings.
Having thus spread out this cloth and worshipped it according to the ritual,
you must ensure that there is abundant rain here for the welfare of the world.
When he had thus prayed, Śāntaśrī heard it;
all the lords of the nāgas promised him, saying, "So be it."
Then that wise knower of mantras, by the command of the Lord of all Nāgas,
having drawn the mandala on a cloth and having consecrated it according to the ritual rules, [proceeded].
Later, when a drought occurred there, for the sake of bringing about good rain,
it was established here in Nāgapura, where it was burnt and then carefully preserved.
Then that Vajrin, the Ācārya, having entreated all those lords of serpents and having shown them discipline, dismissed them while gladdening them.
Then all those nāga kings returned to their respective abodes;
raising up a mass of clouds, they rained everywhere.
Then, due to the occurrence of abundant rain, the famine went to its destruction;
and a state of prosperity, auspiciousness, and enthusiasm prevailed everywhere.
Then all those people, gladdened by great joy and delight,
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, always practiced what is virtuous.
Then that king, the ruler who had seen the truth, being gratified,
duly honored the teacher Śāntiśrī.

Having prostrated with the eight limbs, his soul serene, and having performed circumambulations, he gazed with palms joined in reverence and made this request with great devotion: Svayambhū Purāṇa 8.220.
O Blessed One, Great Teacher, through the power of your Dharma,
all calamities have been pacified and a timely rain has begun to fall.
Therefore, in this place, there shall surely always be freedom from calamity on all sides,
and may there be an uninterrupted surge of the auspiciousness of the glory of the Dharma.
Thus, always beholding my domain with a compassionate eye,
you ought in every way to act so as to ensure it is free from calamity and filled with auspicious energy.
Now my birth and my life in this world have become fruitful,
since all people have become happy as they always move about in auspiciousness.
Therefore, O Teacher, I shall now bear your command upon my head;
having resorted to the stage of life of a sovereign, I shall move about protecting the world.
Having bestowed his favor upon him and being moved by compassion,
he should cause that person's mind to remain steadfast in the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment.
Having thus addressed the Teacher, the protector of the earth bowed at his lotus feet;
having obtained his permission, he returned to the city with great enthusiasm.
There, that king, relying upon his ministers and counselors with joy,
took up the vow of the conduct of awakening and remained performing what is virtuous at all times.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Propagation of the Auspicious Rain of Practice through the Names of the Svayambhū Caitya Hermitages.
Now begins the ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Majesty and Power of the Accomplishment of the Qualities of the Glorious Mahācārya Śāntikara.
Then Maitreya, having looked [upon him], rose up with palms joined in reverence.
Having bowed down to that Blessed One, he made this request with great reverence: Svayambhūpurāṇa 9.1.
When did his name "Śāntikara" come about, and how so?
I wish to hear the cause of that; you should deign to instruct me.
When Maitreya had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing, looking upon that Great Being, gave this instruction: *Svayambhūpurāṇa* 9.3.
Listen, Maitreya, I shall describe the great quality of those possessed of peaceful glory:
the zeal for accomplishing the true Dharma, which bestows the meaningful qualities of auspicious glory upon the virtuous guru.
That king, a great being who longed for the qualities of the True Dharma,
abandoned sensual pleasures and his kingdom to undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
Having bathed in all the sacred fords and having performed acts of giving,
he should practice the threefold concentration and observe the Poṣadha vow.
Thus, wandering through all the sacred seats (pīṭhas) with his mind fixed on the True Dharma,
he practiced the observance of yogic conduct, remaining composed in meditation.
Wandering thus through all the fields of merit, they arrived here;
having seen this delightful maṇḍala, they were filled with wonder.
Having seen this Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Victors, from afar,
he quickly approached with joy to behold it, having prostrated with the eight limbs of reverence.
Having assembled, those great beings, having beheld this realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), which is the abode of the Victors and the form of light, bowed down and took refuge in it.
Then the king, having arrived there in this delightful Nepal,
wandered about everywhere, looking on and observing everything.
Having bathed in all those sacred fords and having given as desired,
perform your vow with a concentrated mind, having undertaken it according to the prescribed rule.
Then, seeing those eight who were free from passion, he was filled with joy;
having propitiated them according to the rules and worshipped them, he constantly paid them homage.
Then that great goddess, having propitiated the great sovereign Khagānanā according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped her, adored her with joy.
Then, having beheld the caitya of Mañjuśrī, he was filled with joy;
having worshipped it according to the prescribed rites, he stood before it and paid homage.
Then, through these great merits, his senses were purified by the glory of peace;
having taken up the vows of renunciation, he became a celibate practitioner.
Because his six sense-faculties were adorned with such supreme tranquility and splendor, he was renowned as Śāntaśrī (Tranquil Glory). Thus it came to pass.
Then that wise Bodhisattva of virtuous mind, for the welfare of the world,
took up the vow of the Vajra-teacher and practiced with concentrated composure.
Then, having covered this Jina Dharmadhātu with a stone slab and having constructed a great stūpa with bricks, he protected it thoroughly.
Then, five deities were established here in the five cities;
this caitya was dedicated to Mañjuśrī, and this great deed was performed by him.
Having thus performed all his duties here, that one of great intelligence,
the Bodhisattva of great supernormal powers, proceeded for the welfare of the world.
Then, having pacified the great calamities on all sides,
he who was ever possessed of peaceful glory brought about auspicious prosperity and joyful exertion.
Then, possessing great supernormal knowledge, he turned back the drought;
having propitiated the nāga kings, he brought about a bountiful rain.
Thus, he who pacifies great calamities through the threefold supernatural knowledges (abhijñā) and always brings about auspiciousness is remembered as Śāntikara.
A mantra-practitioner such as this, a Vajrācārya of great wisdom and great superknowledge,
endowed with prosperity and accomplishments, has never existed before, nor will there ever be one again.
Having thus brought about an auspicious festival free from all calamities everywhere,
that Bodhisattva Śāntaśrī became honored throughout the three worlds.
Thus, having understood this great merit which accomplishes the qualities of auspicious glory, those who seek the wholesome should go for refuge and practice accordingly.
If, having gone to him for refuge and resorted to him with faith, they should always worship him joyfully, propitiating him according to the prescribed rule; Svayambhū Purāṇa 9.28.
All those pure-souled ones, free from afflictions and having conquered their senses,
attained the perfection of the qualities of auspicious glory along with supernatural power and accomplishment.
And those who, always mindful of him and even meditating with concentrated minds, should worship him with faith while constantly reciting his name; Svayambhū Purāṇa 9.30.
May they all be free from blemish, with the three spheres completely purified;
may they possess the glory of those virtues and become practitioners of the path to awakening.
Thus, having understood that his merit is so great, those who seek his virtues should go for refuge to him alone and always worship him with joy.
Thus instructed by the Lord of Sages, all those people gathered in the assembly,
having replied "So be it," were enlightened and rejoiced.
Thus this Great Being bears the noble glory and the meaning of excellent virtues.
Having brought about the welfare of all sentient beings, he remained thus for a very long time.
Then, as time passed, the king, having grown old and his senses decayed, became free from afflictions and detached from worldly objects; meditating, he reflected thus: (Svayambhūpurāṇa 9.35)
"I am old, with limbs exceedingly decayed; how long shall I remain thus? By the power of destiny, I shall certainly and inevitably go to death. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 9.36)
Therefore, in this matter, I ought now to bestow upon my young son this kingdom, together with its consecration, for the protection of the world.
Having reflected thus, that king, having consecrated his son Narendradeva and made him the monarch, instructed him while awakening him to the truth: Svayambhūpurāṇa 9.38.
O King, having established your son and acting according to the principles of righteousness,
and having paid homage to the Three Jewels, always proceed in what is auspicious.
From this day forward, you shall be the sovereign lord of all worlds,
the instructor of all dharmas, and the upholder of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Therefore, in this world, while protecting all people according to the principles of Dharma,
and having paid homage to the Three Jewels, proceed always in auspiciousness.
Having thus instructed his son, that father, free from desire for worldly existence,
abandoned all possessions and took refuge in the forest retreat.
Abiding there, possessing great supernormal knowledge and with the three spheres completely purified,
he established his own mind in meditative absorption and maintained the Brahma-restraint amidst the cycle of existence.
Then, when the time had passed and it was the hour of death, he,
being composed and recollecting the Three Jewels, abandoned his body and went to Sukhāvatī.
Then that king, Narendradeva, like Indra himself,
protected all the worlds with great effort, bringing them to full awakening.
That king, too, being pure of soul and longing for the virtues of the true Dharma,
approached that teacher Śāntikara and went to him for refuge.
There, having taken refuge in that and bearing the Teacher’s command upon his head,
he honored the Three Jewels and always practiced what was virtuous.
Having performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites at all sacred fords (tīrtha) at all times,
he offered funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to his ancestors and gave to supplicants whatever they desired.
Likewise, having duly propitiated the eight Vītarāgas as well as the lords of the world of the Kṣatriyas,
he honored them on the festival days.
And so, having propitiated and worshipped the venerable Mahādevī Khagānanā according to the prescribed rite, he honored her with great enthusiasm and joy.
Likewise, he took refuge at this foremost of shrines of Mañjuśrī,
and having propitiated and worshipped it according to the ritual rules, he venerated it constantly.
Likewise, having duly propitiated and worshipped the deities of Wind along with their retinues in Vāyupura, he always served them.
Likewise, having duly propitiated and worshipped the fire deities along with their retinues in the city of Vahni, he always paid them homage.
Likewise, in Nāgapura, he always worshipped the serpent deities together with their retinues,
having propitiated and honored them according to the prescribed rites.
Likewise, having propitiated and worshipped the goddess Vasudhārā together with her maṇḍala in the city of Vasupura according to the prescribed rite, he constantly venerated her.
Likewise, having propitiated and duly honored the glorious Jina Sambara together with his retinue in Śāntipura according to the ritual rules, he worshipped him constantly.
In that manner, that lord of men relied upon that dharmadhātu;
having propitiated it according to the prescribed rites, he always worshipped and honored it.
Thus that king, the ruler of men, longing for the virtues of the true Dharma,
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, always practiced what is auspicious.
Thus, having diligently awakened all the people to these rites such as pilgrimages to sacred fords, that king proceeded on his conquest.
Likewise, all those people, having accepted the king's command,
proceeded together in these religious pilgrimages and other such rites.
Likewise, the eight who are free from passion, the goddess Khagānanā,
these five deities, and also the caitya of Mañjuśrī.
Having worshipped Jagadīśa, the Lord of the World, the Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Victors, according to the prescribed rites, they always honored him with joy.
By the power of this Dharma, there was always auspiciousness here;
free from calamities and filled with great energy, it proceeded on every side.
Thus that king, the lord of men and god among kings,
having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, proceeded for the welfare of the world.
Likewise, diligently awakening all other worlds as well,
he joined them to the path of enlightenment and set them forth for the welfare of the world.
Thus that king, like Indra, a Bodhisattva and lord of the world,
having accomplished the welfare of all beings, remained for a long time delighting in what is auspicious.
Then that glorious master, the performer of peace, possessed of great supernatural power,
having accomplished his purpose and though advanced in years, did not desire to pass into nirvāṇa.
Desiring the welfare of all sentient beings, he stood at the forefront of the city of peace within a vast meditation hall, which was one *yojana* in measure.
Having raised the great banner of the wish-fulfilling gem upon the glorious,
blazing [stūpa], he is wise, he is a great being, a bodhisattva, a son of the Conquerors.
Absorbed in concentration, dhāraṇīs, vidyās, yoga, and meditation,
he remained with a mind free from wandering, having firmly held the vow for perfect enlightenment.
When this world is bereft of the true Dharma and afflicted by the five degenerations,
he will arise from meditative absorption and teach the true Dharma.
Whenever there was no true spiritual friend, teacher, or lord of knowledge here, at that very time,
there appeared a true spiritual friend, teacher, and lord of knowledge.
Having diligently turned all worlds away from the path of evil and established them on the path to enlightenment, he will cause them to practice the true Dharma.
Having meditated thus, that preceptor Śāntikara,
maintaining his meditative absorption for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, remained poised in the concentration of yoga.
Thus, that teacher of the three qualities, who bears the welfare of all sentient beings,
O Bodhisattva of great supernormal knowledges, remain there for the benefit of the world!
Those who, having gone for refuge to him, always honor him with faith by recollecting, meditating upon, and respectfully uttering even his name.
All those wise Bodhisattvas as well, endowed with great supernormal powers and perfected in auspicious glory and virtues, shall always exist in existence.
Then those pure-souled ones, abiding in the four divine abodes,
having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, will practice for the welfare of the world.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
those Arhats, having attained awakening, will reach the state of the Sugata.
And those who hear the greatness of its qualities with faith and joy,
they too shall attain the perfect accomplishment of the excellence of those qualities.
Having understood this, those who desire the perfection of his virtues ought to listen with reverence to the majesty of his excellent qualities. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 9.81)
Having heard this and other such instructions from the Lord of Sages, all those present in the assembly, being thus awakened, agreed,
saying "So be it," and rejoiced.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Majesty and Power of the Attainment of the Qualities of the Glorious Great Teacher Śāntikara.
Now begins the tenth chapter, titled "The Sūtra of the Sublime Teaching on the Majesty of the Dharma of the Self-Arisen Dharmadhātu.
Then that Blessed One again addressed Maitreya, the Greatly Wise One:
Having surveyed the assembly and addressed them, he commanded as follows:
Listen, Maitreya, I shall speak of the greatness of the qualities of the True Dharma of Mañjuśrī, the Teacher of the World, which bestows the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
This nun Cūḍāsuśīlā, a practitioner of celibacy,
has with faith taken refuge in this shrine of Mañjuśrī.
Having constantly worshipped with garlands of pure blue lotuses according to the prescribed rite,
one should always propitiate [the deity] with devotion and faith, while recollecting and meditating upon it.
I bow to the primordial one at the moving peak with the nine-syllable mantra "svāhā";
she who always worships while reciting this supreme vidyā-dhāraṇī. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 10.5)
By the power of this merit, the nun Cūṇḍī will certainly become possessed of the five superknowledges within twelve years.
Then, this great supernormal knowledge, which is the locus of the qualities of glorious prosperity,
shall act for the benefit of all sentient beings and practice the vow of awakening.
Then the Arhatī, possessed of great wisdom and with the three spheres completely purified,
having attained the threefold awakening, shall reach the state of a Perfect Buddha.
In this way, others in the three worlds as well, reciting this dhāraṇī at the shrine of Mañjuśrī, always honor it with faith.
They too were all free from blemish, with the three spheres completely purified;
they were Bodhisattvas who had conquered their senses, the repositories of auspicious glory and excellent virtues.
Having attained the state of the five superknowledges and practicing the four divine abodes,
may they act according to the bodhisattva vow, serving as a support for the welfare of all sentient beings.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
they conquered all the hosts of Māra, becoming free from afflictions with stainless faculties.
Even Arhats, possessing great supernormal powers and devoted to the means of attaining perfect enlightenment,
may reach the three types of enlightenment and thereby attain the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Thinking, "You too [should do so]," likewise venerate this Mañjuśrī-caitya here while reciting this dhāraṇī, you who possess the aspiration for awakening.
For you all, too, being anointed with this merit and having purified the three spheres,
shall likewise become sons of the Sugata.
Bodhisattvas, who are the locus of auspicious glory and excellent virtues, possess great supernormal knowledges; as lords of the world, they shall become practitioners of the auspicious conduct.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for perfect enlightenment in due order,
and having conquered all the hosts of Māra, he dwelt in the four divine abodes.
"Having attained the threefold awakening, you shall become Buddhas"—if you desire perfect enlightenment, recognize this as the truth. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 10.18)
"Always worship this stūpa of Mañjuśrī with joy!
Having heard these and other words thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, they, together with their assembly, [acted accordingly].
Having been thus enlightened, all the worlds, including Brahmā, Śakra, and the other immortals, said, "So be it," and rejoiced. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 10.20)
All the lords of the world, together with their retinues, were filled with joy and,
being thoroughly inspired with faith, [honored] that Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, along with his Saṅgha.
Having bowed down and performed circumambulations, all the mortals— the king and others, together with their ministers, country-folk, and citizens— joyfully departed for their respective abodes.
Having bowed to that Lord of Munis together with his retinue, they went to their respective abodes;
and Hārītī, the queen of the Yakṣiṇīs, along with her sons, became a protector of the Buddhists.
Having made an offering to the Three Jewels and taken refuge in the form of the Dharmadhātu,
that Blessed One then arose together with his assembly of monks.
Illuminating the world with his radiance, he went to the hermitage of Jaṭodyāna;
there, the Lord of the three worlds suddenly engaged in sport with thousands of women.
"Having fully taught the True Dharma, he dwelt for the welfare of the world"—
thus was it instructed by my Guru, which I have heard and relate accordingly.
"Having heard this, O Great King, approve it with faith.
Having thus heard what was taught by the Teacher, the Arhat, that lord of men [acted accordingly].
Having been thus propitiated, he bowed to that Arhat and spoke with reverence:
"Venerable sir, I desire to see that Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) for myself."
"I shall not go to Nepal; grant me your permission for that.
Having heard this request made by the king, the Arhat Ārhaṇyatī rejoiced.
Beholding that king, the Great Being spoke thus:
"Excellent, O King! If you so desire, [seek] that Self-Existent One."
Go to see him; having propitiated him, worship him endowed with faith, and having bathed in all the sacred fords, give gifts according to your desire.
Having propitiated and worshipped with respectful devotion the passionless Mahādevī Dharmodayā, who has the face of a bird and is the sovereign of the Jinas; SvayambhuP_10.32.
Having taken refuge with faith and having worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, venerate with devotion the five deities residing in the five cities.
Having propitiated and fully honored him, worship him with devotion and respect;
and likewise, behold the shrine of Mañjuśrī according to the prescribed rite.
Having propitiated and fully honored the teacher, who is seated in a cave and established in meditative absorption and dhyāna, one should worship him while reciting this dhāraṇī.
Having meditated upon, propitiated, fully honored, and bowed to [him], worship him with great reverence;
likewise, [worship] the other Great Beings who are worshippers of the Dharmadhātu.
Having propitiated and honored all [the Buddhas] and having paid homage to them,
Bhadraśrī— whose self was purified by this merit and who was a repository of excellent qualities— [attained his goal].
The Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, shall even become the protectors of the world;
thereafter, having fulfilled the equipment for perfect enlightenment, they proceed in due order.
"Having attained arhatship, you shall reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha"—if you desire perfect awakening, recognize this as the truth. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 10.39)
Having gone there with great enthusiasm and beheld that Dharmadhātu,
propitiate him according to the prescribed rites and remain devoted to him as your refuge.
Go; may there be auspiciousness for you, and may your desire be fulfilled.
Having beheld [the deity] according to your wish, return filled with joy.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, the king, with joy,
bowed with palms joined to that Guru and, having received his permission, rejoiced.
Then that king, the lord of men, together with his ministers, countryfolk, and citizens, set forth joyfully, accompanied by royal splendor, auspicious rites, and great enthusiasm.
There, O Indra among kings, gladdening all the worlds as he proceeded with great energy along that path, he quickly arrived at Nepāla.
Having arrived there and beheld that glorious Svayambhū from afar, one should,
with a joyful mind, quickly perform a prostration with palms joined in reverence.
Having observed everywhere there that which was set in motion by auspicious enthusiasm,
the king approached those who were filled with wonder and joy.
There, having bathed in all the sacred fords in succession, that lord of men gave gifts to those in need according to their desires, while practicing his vow.

Then, seeing those eight who were free from passion, the king was filled with joy; having honored them according to the prescribed rite, he worshipped and served them according to the prescribed rite.
Then, acting with joy, having beheld the dharmadhātu, the abode of the Victors,
he propitiated it according to the ritual rules and, having worshipped it thoroughly, he venerated it in due order.
Then, having joyfully propitiated and worshipped the deity Vāyu together with his retinue in Vāyupura according to the prescribed rite, he paid homage to him.
Then, in the city of Agni, having worshipped and honored the fire-deities along with their retinues according to the prescribed rites, he devoted himself to them with reverence.
Then, in Nāgapura, the Nāga deities together with their retinues,
having propitiated and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, honored him with joy.
Then, having propitiated the goddess Śrī Vasundharā together with her retinue in Vasupura according to the prescribed ritual, he worships and honors her with great devotion.
Then, having propitiated and worshipped the glorious Saṃvara along with his retinue according to the ritual rules in Śāntipura, he venerated him with joy.
Then, having meditated upon the preceptor Śāntikara as he remained established in meditative absorption,
and having propitiated and honored him, they worshipped him with great joy.
Then the goddess Dharmmodayā, having propitiated and worshipped the great sovereign Khagānanā according to the prescribed rite, honored her with joy.
I pay homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, the lotus-eyed, the omniscient one who is the abode of compassion,
the Teacher Samantabhadra, the Lion of the Śākyas.
I bow to Śrīghana, the glorious and most excellent one, the mass of virtue who brings auspiciousness;
to the illustrious one who bestows glory, the peaceful one who is the very embodiment of peace.
I bow to the lion who proclaims selflessness, who is blameless and free from outflows, who knows the right method, whose self is stainless, and who is without blemish.
I bow to the Tathāgata, who is free from dualities, free from egoism, free from conceptual construction,
who has shaken off all afflictions, and who is beyond all worldly proliferation.
I bow to Viśveśvara, the particular self, the universal-formed Vināyaka,
who is complete with all characteristics and free from passion.
I bow to Viśveśa, who is endowed with the most excellent conduct, possesses stainless radiance,
has subdued his impulses, is pure, and is free from delusion.
I pay homage to the tamer of the wicked, the peaceful, the pure, the abode of the five Victors, the Sugata of excellent renown, the gentle one of radiant fame.
I pay homage to the Lord of Yogins, who possesses the ten powers, who knows the world,
who is worshipped by the world, who is the teacher of the world, who is the embodiment of the world, and the protector of the worlds.
I bow to Him who is free from blemish, the enemy of desire, the one who possesses all qualities, the bearer of the digits [of the moon],
whose form is beautiful, the object of compassion, and who has the luster of gold.
Then, taking refuge in the Dharmadhātu at the caitya of Mañjuśrī,
he propitiated it according to the ritual rules, worshipped it thoroughly, and paid homage with devotion.
Then, moving with joy and beholding the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the abode of the Victors,
he propitiated it according to the ritual rules and worshipped it with great delight.
With supreme devotion, he praised the self-arisen abode of the Jina:
"Homage to you, who are the form of consciousness for that which is of the nature of light."

Salutations to you, O beloved of your devotees, who brought about the destruction of Mura and others, who bestows prosperity, who takes the form of the Praṇava, and whose form faces in all directions.
Salutations to the creator of the elements such as earth, who is worthy of worship by the world;
salutations again and again to the creator of the universe, the protector of the universe, and the sustainer of the universe.
Having thus praised him who is attainable through meditation, who is the object of meditation, and who bestows the fourfold aims of life, Aśoka then performed an act of seeking forgiveness.
Thus that king, having honored and venerated all those great beings who were lay practitioners of the dharmadhātu, fully satisfied them.
Thus that king, the lord of men, relying upon the form of the glorious Dharmadhātu,
performed worship to the Three Jewels and practiced the bodhisattva vow.
Then that king, together with his ministers, country-folk, and citizens,
having bowed and circumambulated the Dharmadhātu, proceeded joyfully.
Then, traveling about, that lord of the earth, gladdened by great enthusiasm,
suddenly reached the city and entered the monastery.
Having approached that Arhat Upagupta together with his assembly,
and having observed him, he bowed with palms joined and withdrew to a secluded spot.
Beholding him arrived, the Teacher, worthy of honor, with a serene gaze, asked the king: "Welcome; I hope you are well?"
Having heard that, the protector of the earth, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to the Teacher;
with a most serene countenance and gazing upon him, he spoke thus: *Svayambhū Purāṇa* 10.78.
I have come here, O Teacher, through the power of your compassion;
how could my welfare not be secured everywhere and at all times?
By the power of your grace, I have wandered joyfully through Nepal,
visiting all the sacred sites, bathing therein, and giving gifts as desired.
Likewise, having observed the eight who are free from passion, being heedful,
he should duly propitiate and worship them in succession according to their lineage.
Then, having beheld that glorious Svayambhū, the source of all phenomena (dharmadhātu),
they propitiated him according to the prescribed rites, honored him, and worshipped him with joy.
Then, in Vāyupura, the deity Vāyu was worshipped by me;
thereafter, in Agnipura, the deity Agni was also worshipped by me.
Likewise, in Nāgapura, the nāga kings were worshipped by me;
and similarly, in Vasupura, the goddess Vasundharā was duly honored.
Then, in Śāntipura, the glorious Saṃvara was worshipped;
thereafter, the preceptor Śāntikara was beheld and worshipped by me.
Having propitiated the goddess Khagānanā and worshipped her,
he also worshipped the caitya of Mañjuśrī according to the prescribed rites.
Thus, O Venerable One, there at Upacchandoha on that ground of merit,
I worshipped all the gods according to the prescribed ritual.
This merit has been obtained by me through the power of your grace;
therefore, my birth and my life are now truly fruitful.
Likewise, O Teacher, always remembering the dharmadhātu here, the abode of the Victors, reciting its name and meditating upon it, may I worship it; may there be no further existence.
Having heard what was thus related by the king, he, being pleased and worthy of honor,
looked at the monarch and commanded him once again as follows.
You are fortunate that, having recollected and meditated upon the Dharmadhātu, the abode of the Victors, you desire to venerate it; therefore, always worship it here.
With a self purified by this merit, a refuge for the excellent qualities of auspicious glory,
may you become a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the sovereign of all dharmas.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for perfect enlightenment in due order, you,
as an Arhat, will attain the three types of awakening and certainly reach the state of a Buddha.
Even by merely hearing the account of the origin of that self-arisen Dharmadhātu, one obtains great merit which is the means for achieving perfect awakening.
Thinking thus, mortals should in every way listen with reverence and faith to this account of the origin of that Self-Existent One.
Those people who, with devotion, respect, faith, and joy, listen to the account of the origin of that self-arisen Dharmadhātu, [attain the supreme state].
They never go to an evil rebirth anywhere at any time;
always born in a happy state of existence, they are the locus of auspicious glory and excellent virtues.
May these sons of the Sugata become lords of the world, possessing great superknowledges and delighting in the vow of the bodhisattva conduct that brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having gradually fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment for the welfare of the world,
may they attain the threefold awakening of an Arhat and reach the state of a Sugata.

Thinking thus, O Great King, those who desire awakening should listen with faith and reverence to this majesty of the qualities of the Self-Existent One, which is difficult to encounter. (SvayambhuP 10.100)

Those men who listen with devotion, respect, faith, and joy to this [work] which bestows the meaning of the virtues of the glory of the True Dharma and the majesty of the qualities of the Self-Existent One; SvayambhuP_10.101.
They too shall not go to an evil rebirth, but shall always be joined to a good rebirth;
becoming vessels for auspicious glory and excellent virtues, they shall attain awakening.
Therefore, having heard this great merit, having meditated upon it with constant devotion,
and having recollected and uttered its name, one should worship the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū).
O King, in the past, having heard a discourse on the excellent qualities of the self-existent Dharmadhātu, I too became filled with great joy.
Then I suddenly arrived there in Nepal;
having bathed in all the sacred fords, I gave gifts according to my desire.
Having propitiated those eight who were free from passion, they were honored by me;
and having also propitiated the goddess Khagānanā, she too was duly worshipped.
Having propitiated and worshipped the caitya of Mañjuśrī,
five deities who had previously resided there were also worshipped.
Likewise, the preceptor Śāntikara, having been beheld and duly honored,
then took refuge in the self-arisen Dharmadhātu.
Always honoring with faith and joyfully propitiating [the teacher],
one who thus constantly relies upon that [teacher] is a worshiper of the dharmadhātu.
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, they practiced the vow of awakening;
thus, with their selves purified by this merit, they were completely pure in the three spheres.
"Having attained awakening, may I now become a son of the Conquerors in this world"—realizing this, those humans desire perfect nirvāṇa. (Svayambhūpurāṇa 10.111)
Having propitiated the Dharmadhātu, they should always worship it with joy,
by recollecting it, meditating upon it, and respectfully uttering its name.
Having beheld and even prostrated before it, let them worship that abode of the Jinas;
those who always worship the abode of the Jinas by recollecting, meditating upon, and bowing down to it.
"Having swiftly attained perfect awakening, may they reach the state of a fully enlightened Buddha"—
this truth has been proclaimed by all the lords of sages.
Having heard and rejoiced in that realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and having recollected it, let them fully devote themselves to it;
and those who, having heard this well-spoken word, possess a mind of sympathetic joy.
Having recollected and meditated upon the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), they always pay homage;
they too possess this great merit and the complete purity of the three spheres.
The Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, possessors of auspicious glory and the foundation of excellent qualities, who dwell in the four Brahma-abodes,
are endowed with great supernormal powers and pure faculties.
"Having swiftly attained awakening, may they reach the state of a Perfect Buddha"—
this was instructed by my Guru, and having heard it, I speak thus.
You too, O people, should always cause this to be heard and rejoice in it;
by the power of this merit, may you always and everywhere [prosper].
"Without doubt, the lord of men will surely experience auspicious vigor free from calamity.
Having heard this prediction from that Arhat, King Aśoka was filled with joy.
Having replied, "So be it," he rejoiced along with his retinue;
then all those people, having heard this well-spoken word, [were filled with joy].
Having rejoiced with great enthusiasm, they always proceeded toward what is auspicious;
then, by the power of that merit, it was everywhere and at all times there.
"May there be no calamities and may auspicious enthusiasm proceed without interruption"—
having thus commanded, that one of great wisdom, Jayaśrī, possessed of great supernormal knowledge, [spoke].
Beholding all those members of the assembly, he again instructed them thus:
"Wherever this discourse on the Dharma should be set forth, even in the Kali age."
Whoever hears it after it has been spoken, whoever causes others to hear it, or whoever propagates it—
for all of these, the Perfectly Awakened Ones are always present there in their entirety.
Beholding them with a compassionate gaze, may they bring about well-being until the end of existence;
and may all the goddesses who are the perfections (pāramitās) always grant auspiciousness to them there.
Having completed the equipment for perfect enlightenment, may all the bodhisattvas as well as the solitary sugatas fulfill it in due order.
May the Arhats and yogis always bestow auspiciousness upon them,
as well as all the lords of the world and all the great seers.
In that regard, all the lords of the gods and even all the lords of the Daityas should perform auspicious rites for them all after due consideration.
Likewise, all the gandharvas, all the lords of the yakṣas,
the garuḍas, the nāga kings, and even the sovereigns of the kumbhāṇḍas [were present].
Having observed them always, all the Mātṛkā goddesses, together with the hosts of Bhairavas, should provide protection for them on every side.
Having always performed protection for them,
may all the grahas, the stars, the siddhas, and even the vidyādharas bring about well-being on every side.
Having always observed those who are to be converted, they should perform what is most auspicious for them;
so too shall the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and even the wicked hosts of Māra.
Having seen them, those [deities] will always joyfully provide protection;
and whoever joyfully writes down this discourse on the greatness of the qualities of the Self-Existent One, [shall likewise receive their favor].
By him all the well-spoken teachings of the Mahāyāna were written down,
and by him this well-spoken discourse on the Dharmadhātu was caused to be inscribed.
By that person as well, the entire Sūtra would certainly have been caused to be written;
and whoever has written this and established it according to the prescribed rite [shall likewise attain merit].
Having placed it in a pure location within the house and always worshipped it with the requisites of worship,
by that [act], all the Arhats, Jinas, and even the Pratyekabuddhas [are honored].
Indeed, the Bodhisattvas together with their Saṅgha become honored by those who,
having themselves upheld this [teaching], also instruct others in it.
One should constantly cultivate [the practice] by recollecting and meditating upon it, and should prostrate with joy;
for all the lords of sages and even the individual Sugatas [revere] him.
The Arhats and Bodhisattvas, being pleased, shall grant whatever is desired,
as shall the one who teaches this [mantra] and all the Śrāvakas as well.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, he should satisfy them with offerings;
by that, all the perfectly awakened Buddhas as well as the Pratyekabuddhas are satisfied.
All the monks are arhats, practitioners of yoga, and observers of the holy life;
and all the bodhisattvas are likewise observers of vows and ascetics.
If they are honored, fed, satisfied, and rejoiced in, then all the Buddhas, the lords of sages, will likewise be so; what need is there for much speaking?
All the Tārās, the goddesses, and all the assemblies of the sons of the Victors constantly look upon them with compassion and rejoice in them.
Having performed protection everywhere, they should grant the desired boon.
All the lords of the world, as well as all the gods and lords of the asuras,
having provided protection, shall grant boons to those who strive for the accomplishment of the True Dharma.
Even kings, having always provided protection for them and expressed their approval,
shall protect them with constant devotion, granting whatever they desire.
Their ministers as well— along with their councilors, secretaries, attendants, servants, armies, and warriors— should always act for their benefit.
May all the Vaiśyas be sustainers of all interests and dear to their friends;
may all the merchants and great men be doers of good.
Even enemies would become servants, and those who have been seen would come to have intentions for one's welfare;
likewise, all other people as well would possess minds of loving-kindness.
Beasts, birds, all insects, and living creatures—none of these shall be hostile toward them; rather, they shall be proclaimers of their welfare.
Thus, in all worlds, for those who accomplish the true Dharma, there shall always be an absence of calamities,
auspicious exertion, and constant well-being.
Thus, having bowed to that Lord of the Three Worlds, who is the source of the most excellent merit arising from the realm of the Self-Existent One, worship him always with joy. (SvayambhuP 10.153)
Those who, having taken refuge in him, remain concentrated through mindfulness and meditation, and who always worship him with faith while even uttering his name; SvayambhūP_10.154 //
Their three jewels are always perfectly serene;
looking upon them with a compassionate gaze, they shall always bestow what is auspicious.
Thus, what was commanded by the Śāstra is heard by Jayaśrī;
the entire assembly, headed by Jineśvarī, has been awakened and gladdened.
The entire assembly, having heard this, was thoroughly pacified;
responding with "So be it," they were awakened and offered their joyful praise.
Then all those people, having risen up and being gratified,
bowed to Jayaśrī together with the Saṅgha and departed for their respective hermitages.
There, having approached constantly with great supernatural power together with his retinue and the sons of the Conqueror,
they all bathed in every sacred ford and observed their vows according to the prescribed rule.
Then, according to the prescribed rite, he worshipped the eight Vītarāgas, the goddess Khagānanā, and the five deities as well.
Likewise, having propitiated the Dharmadhātu, he always venerated the Caitya of Śāntikarācārya and also that of Mañjuśrī, after meditating upon and worshipping them.
Then, through the power of that merit, in that realm there was always an absence of calamities and a flourishing of auspicious energy on all sides.
Then that son of the Sugata, Jayaśrī, possessed of great supernormal powers, beholding all those members of the assembly, again gave this instruction: Svayambhūpurāṇa 10.163.
Wherever this discourse on the Dharma of the Self-Existent One is propagated,
may there always be auspiciousness through the power of that merit.
May all the Perfectly Awakened Ones there, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas,
Arhats, and Bodhisattvas, always bestow auspiciousness.
May all the lords of the world and all the great ṛṣis,
always beholding [this] there, perform what is most auspicious.
May the clouds rain in due season, may the earth be rich in crops,
and may there always be freedom from calamity and abundance of food in that place.
May the king be most righteous, may the ministers follow the path of policy,
and may all people abide in virtuous conduct and accomplish the Dharma.
May all beings, conducting themselves with propriety and possessing intentions directed toward perfect enlightenment,
honor the Three Jewels and always proceed in what is auspicious.
Having heard what was thus instructed by Jayaśrī, all the members of the assembly said,
"So be it," and being gratified, they rejoiced.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the Sūtra of Sublime Sayings on the Greatness of the Dharma of the Self-Arisen Dharmadhātu.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; thus speaks the Great Śramaṇa.
May there be auspiciousness.
